House resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Fielding for Committee of Supply and the proposed amendment of Mr. Foster thereto.
Mr. j. E. ARMSTRONG (East Lambton). Mr. 'Speaker, in rising to support the resolution I heartily congratulate the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster) upon the a >ie manner in which he has placed his facts and figures before the House and the non-partisan way in which he has dealt with the question. We appreciate the work the lion, gentleman (Mr. Foster) did in gathering such valuable information, and I hope that every member of this House agrees with him that civil service appointments should be filled only on account of merit and after proper examination. The words of Gladstone, quoted by the hon. gentleman, ought to be convincing, and ought to teach us that we should no longer continue in our present slipshod and haphazard manner of conducting the affairs of the country. The hon. gentleman referred to the superannuation system and the necessity of making it part of our civil service-law. The patronage system has been one of the greatest curses to the civil service, and the sooner it is done away with the better for the country at large. The report of the Civil Service Commission has distinctly laid it down that improvement must be along the lines of securing better examinations and granting greater powers in dealing with the civil service. The report of that commission confirms the view of the member for North Toronto that partisan favouritism and puli are largely the cause of the irregularities which have occurred in the civil service. The money which this Dominion receives from the people of Canada is largely expended through the instrumentality of the civil service and hence the necessity for an honest and competent staff in every public department. 1 regret that the Minister of Finance was rather inclined to introduce party politics into the discussion. It may be true, as he said that the evils in the civil service are not peculiar to the present administration, but if he compares the report of the Civil Service Commission of 1892 with the report of the last Civil Service Commission, I am sure the comparison will not be satisfactory to him. On the very first page of the last Civil Service Commissioner's report I find :

The commissioners report that in the short and possibly inadequate feme at their disposal it has become very evident that in the present state of the development of Canada important changes are required to maintain the civil service as an efficient, contented and useful part of the machinery of administrative government.
On page 11 the commissioners state :
The commissioners also heg to point out that besides a certificate of good health no person should he admitted to examinations unless his character is such as to qualify him for employment in the service. As only one certificate as regards moral character is required by the Board of Civil Service Examiners it is quite within the bounds of possibility that there may be collusion between the candidate and the giver of the certificate.
On page 13 the commissioners make use of this strong language :
Prom the inquiries made by the commissioners and the evidence submitted to them, they are constrained to declare that they are unable to agree with the expression of opinion contained in the order of reference, and they are of opinion that the repeal of the Act is really the best course to pursue in the public interest. What should be given in its place the commissioners will state when they come to that part of the report in which they make recommendations.
Suffice it to say that the strongest possible condemnation of tbe_ present administration of the civil service of Canada can be founu within the pages of this report. As representatives of the people we cannot too soon provide a remedy for the evils therein pointed out. We need not only a strict civil service law but we need a civil service commission of independent men who will not only look after the interests of the civil service hut the interests of every department of government as well. We need a purchasing board ; a board not composed of party politicians who will purchase supplies for the government under the wretched patronage system that has prevailed for the last number of years, but of men who in purchasing these supplies will always keep in mind the best interests of the people of the whole Dominion who contribute the money. The resolution before tbe House deserves our enthusiastic support. It is universally admitted that those who were leaders of the country in the earlier years had not to contend with many of the evils of the present day. Corruption now seems to be an element in the daily administration of our affairs. Partisan tyranny and debasement, the outgrowth of contention for patronage, office and power, were almost unknown in years gone by, whereas to-day they run riot throughout tbe land.

['I have the honour to inform the House that I have received from Armand Lavergne, Esq., his resignation as member for the electoral district of Mont-magny, and that I have issued my warrant to the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery to make out a new writ of election for the said electoral district.']
Why do you not read the civil service report ?
Does the hon. gentleman wish me to read more from that report ?
Certainly, and wake up.

I shall he able to accommodate the hon. gentleman in that regard before I have concluded my remarks. The patronage system is now recognized as a great problem in our public affairs, and I believe the Prime Minister recognizes that fact. There is not a minister administering a department who does not recognize that to the patronage system, and to party interests he has to devote a large part of the valuable time which under good government should be devoted to the interests of the country. Pew thoughtful men are so blind as not to see that a great reform is essential to prevent a great national calamity. Older nations have found that good methods, clean administration, honest, wise, prudent, faithful, men of worth and capacity in the civil service, demand the serious attention of their legislators. Intrigues, bribery and want of principle hung over the administration of public affairs in Great Britain and the United States before the introduction of radical civil service reform. In a young country such as ours abuses will naturally grow as our wealth accumulates, our population increases and the duties and responsibilities of public men multiply.
Therefore it is our bounden duty as members of parliament to put on the statute-book a civil service reform law that will be of benefit to our people and our public men, who to-day, from the Prime Minister down to the latest addition on the government side, squander much of their time in looking after the political aspirants in their constituencies instead of devoting their efforts to the public good. The people of Canada have little to say in running this country. The Prime Minister has more power than a king. He appoints the men in his cabinet. They in turn appoint civil servants. He appoints members to the bench. He appoints commissioners and representatives in foreign lands. He appoints members of parliament to positions of emolument. He appoints men to the Senate. He appoints lieutenant governors and is credited with appointing premiers in some of the provinces. Members and ministers under him in many instances are afraid to assert their rights for fear of losing patronage in their ridings and their positions as members of parliament. While reforms have been carried on in other lands, we in Canada have continued our careless and almost reckless policy. I firmly believe that the day is not far distant when a radical change must take place. These abuses must be removed. The man who says no is not acquainted with the proper meaning of our constitution or the kind of people who compose our nation. We as a country must realize that peace, prosperity and the general advancement of our interests de-

pend not only on the men in high places, but on the fidelity and ability of those in the public service, down to the very lowest. We must not let prejudice or partisan interests stand in the way of improvements to our civil service. Let us make searching investigation into every department, and obtain information from other countries so that we may have the best system available, and do it now. The surest way to correct abuses is to investigate and expose them. No business man can carry on a successful, business with loose methods and careless administration such as has been exposed in the departments of this government. Prussia set an example by investigating her civil service in 1815. France followed in 1830. Great Britain made a thorough investigation of the civil service in 1854. The United States made a thorough investigation in 1879 and since that.time, but Canada in 1908 is still following the abandoned principles of the 18th century. During the last three quarters of a century a complete revolution has taken place in the civil service of other countries. Rigorous and impartial rests of qualifications have been applied to civil servants and where formerly incompetency, routine and peculation were uppermost, efficiency and fidelity have taken their place. The prosperity and development of -Canada will largely depend on our civil servants, for they materially assist in developing our resources and by public economy and good judgment husband our strength. The civil servants should not be instruments to serve the ends of any political party. It should be our pride and ambition to make the standard of our civil servants so high that each department could be pointed to as conducted and carried on by servants of superior character and capacity. The conduct of the civil service in Great Britain at the time of the war with the United States is largely blamed for the loss of the country to the south of us. If the United States could take out of the quagmire of corrupt poltical influence, the civil service of that country, and place it where it is to-day, surely we with our small population, are not going to say that we are helpless to deal with this question. When you see prominent politicians of both parties fti the United States favouring advanced legislation in regard to the civil service, when you see the presidents one after another promoting civil service reform, and vieing with each other to carry it forward, and when you find that under the present civil service system the people of the United States are able to save on the average $10,000,000 a year, we in Canada should at least take into consideration whether it is not possible for us to remedy the defects that exist in our civil service system. Public administration in Great Britain is reduced to a science, having its principles, methods, theories, tests of character and capacity, along with responsibilities, so Mr. ARMSTRONG.
arranged that the officer dare not depart from these principles. The abuses we have in Canada to-day were endured half a century ago by other nations and the arguments used by this government were used then in defence of similar abuses. The most important lessons -a nation can learn from its own history are to be found in the exposure of its own errors. Surely we have had sufficient historical facts dealing with the careless conduct of our civil servants to warrant a progressive step towards reform. No excuse can be offered why the basis of our civil service should not have as high a position as that of any other nation. If we think our methods perfect and allow false pride and conceit to stand between our duty, and self inspection, we shall continue to Ije blind to the peril of a decline in the moral and intellectual tone of our official life. If partisan leaders, and political majorities are to be the domineering spirit of our national life, then will the voice of truth be silenced and our nation drift on to a day when there will be a national awakening, and our people rise to curse the men who for party gain who were afraid to undertake a reform that woulil elevate our people and place us in the front rank of the nations of the world on this important subject. Look at our position from an outsider's standpoint and compare our advances in civil service reform with those other nations, and we will feel humiliated.
The hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) tried to show this afternoon that the civil service of to-day was fully up to the standard of 1892. But let him take the civil service report of 1892 and compare it with the last report and he cannot help being convinced that the standard of the service, as a whole, is not an enviable one and that instead of the service growing better from year to year it is being undermined by the party system of patronage and is growing worse.
In 1825 public offices in Great Britain were purchasable like merchandise in the markets, also offices in the army, state and church. This practice was stopped in 1871. Read the history of the civil service Reforms in Great Britain, it is a history of struggles to gain positions they hold today. From 1834 to 1868 both parties seem to think that a strictly partisan system of administration was no longer practical and from) that day it was doomed, and any party trying to resurrect it would court defeat.
Why cannot we, as two great political parties, deal with this question on its merits and deal with it quickly? Are our offices public trust for the common good or are they partisan outposts for the special benefit of those who can capture them? I gee before me the ex-Minister of Railways (Mr. Emmerson) and I well remember when a few years he practically defined his position as minister by stating that in the appointment of any man on the Intercolonial Rail-

way, even down to the very navvies, he would take into consideration the interests, of his party and not the welfare of the country. Surely we cannot expect from the civil service the best return if we allow party system to be carried on in the way I have pointed out.
Should parties seek the approval of the people by their strength of a sound policy and principles, or should they seek it through patronage and manipulation of elections? Should members of parliament grasp all the patronage possible and use it to discharge election pledges or partisan spoils and political intrigue? Should members come here free from these incumbrances and devote their energies to promote the welfare of the Dominion pr should they come merely to look after the patronage in their riding? These are questions we should deal with. We are not living in the 17th century, neglecting to educate our people and denying them the right to vote. We are in the blaze of public opinion; we are public servants of a reading, writing, thinking people who do not say to their members: Go to Ottawa and devote your time and talents towards planning and scheming to get your friends into office whether they are competent or not. They do say : Devote your time and talents towards improving legislation ; see that the money is properly expended, that our people are not over-taxed, and that the civil servants are doing their duty. If appointments were to be increased in Canada one hundred fold, is it not clear that party struggles would be still more bitter and politics more corrupt than they are to-day? Is it not wise, therefore, that we should consider the question at present and deal with it effectively? Should we not make a determined effort to rid the politics of this country of the patronage system and clear the civil service of this dead weight on its efficiency? Were we to do this, not only would members on the government side be greatly benefited, but the ministers would have more time to devote to the public interest. For every person or faction conciliated by an appointment there are generally speaking many offended who sought the appointment. Any party relying on patronage and spoils and not on the basis of principle and good administration is not worthy of the confidence of our people and must suffer defeat. The duty of a member of parliament is plain; he should have a constant regard for the old laws of the land, and also see the need of new ones for the common welfare of the people.
This resolution may appear to the government side a new and radical step towards civil service reform, but I feel satisfied that if we should take that step, the duties of the Public Accounts Committee would be to a considerable extent done away with, because there would no longer
be abuses in the departments of this government, the exposures of which have taken up so much of the time of that committee. Instead of the members of the government devoting their independence, dignity, time and talents to their duties as representatives of the people and parliamentarians, we find them in many instances devoting them to party patronage and becoming really patronage brokers. They go from office to office, begging or bullying. To-day it is one thing, to-morrow another. To make a place to-day perhaps for a needy dependent or perhaps an unscrupulous supporter seems to be their chief duty in public life. Departments are beseiged and the time of the officials wasted, while if we had civil service reform that would be largely done away with.
You should stop it.

My hon. friend is not one of the men who want to stop things of that kind. He is one of the men who believes in opening the door to the grafters and boodlers and heelers. He is the very man who can stand up in the Public Accounts Committee and defend the civil servants of this country in not furnishing the people with the information they should. There is no man more ready and willing to defend this government in its nefarious transactions than the hon. gentleman. I am not, therefore, surprised to see him averse to taking any part in considering a resolution of this kind which is for the general benefit of our people.
As members of parliament they hold the pistol of their prestige at the heads of departments, and the result in many cases is to force into the public service such of their relations or friends to become a drain on the treasury for the rest of their lives. Were such officials compelled to undergo a preliminary examination, conducted by an independent and competent board of examiners, this could not happen.
From whom is my hon. friend (Mr. Armstrong) quoting ?

I am quoting from my own knowledge of what is going on in the departments of this government. And, as the ex-Minister of Railways (Mr. Em-merson) well knows, a large portion of his own time, when in office, was taken up with men who were begging and bullying him for appointments on the Intercolonial. He knows that the time of members on his side was largely taken up with this patronage system.
I am afraid the hon. gentleman is drawing on his imagination.

I am not ; I am drawing on the actual experience of the ex-Minister of Railways himself. He knows that he felt compelled to defend in this

House the system of appointing none but politicians to positions on the Intercolonial. He knows that, never during the time that he was in charge of that railway, did he ever appoint any hut partisans to positions in that service. And when we find ministers of the Crown ready to defend the system of party spoil and party pull, we cannot expect from them a Civil Service Bill that will institute reforms of great benefit to the people.
Members having this power make promises for votes and the results are fre

 quently disastrous. Official life is lowered and manv of our best men do not offer themselves for parliamentary honours, owing to the results that inevitably follow. Patronage distribution by members tends to bring the public service into disrepute and has a tendency to convert public officers into active politicians.
Mr. Speaker, I rise to a point of order. I draw your attention to the fact that the hon. gentleman (Mr. Armstrong) is reading his speech.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Of course, the rule is plain ; an hon. member is not permitted to read his speech.

The statements 1 have made within the last five minutes have been mainly dealing with the exMinister of Railways and others on the government side of the House. I have a number of notes to which I wish to refer, and I think it is for the general good that they should be placed before the House. X am surprised that the ex-Minister of Railways (Mr. Emmerson) should take such a decided stand in this regard. Perhaps he will allow me to read the words of the Earl of Duft'erin on the civil service. In a speech delivered in Toronto, he dealt with the civil service. He said :
But, after .all, the chief danger against which you have to guard is that which concerns the civil service of the country. Now, the civil service of the country, though not the animating spirit, is the living mechanism through which the body politic moves, and breathes and has its being. Upon it depends the rapid and economical conduct of every branch of your affairs; and there is nothing about which a nation should be so particular as to secure in such a service, independence, zeal, patriotism and integrity.
Perhaps, the hon. member for Bellechasse (Mr. Talbot) might take note of these remarks of the Earl of Dufferin.
But, in order that this should be the case, it is necessary that the civil servants should be given a status regulated by their requirements, their personal qualifications, their capacity for rendering the country efficient service, and that neither their original appointment nor their subsequent advance should in any way depend upon their political connections or opinions.
Would the hou. gentleman give us the date of that speech ?
The date was September 24, 1878.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Just the time the Conservatives came into power ; and to the day they went out of power they did not introduce any reform Bill.
That is a very broad statement for the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) to make. He knows that he has before him the Civil Service Bill of 1892. He held it up before us this afternoon.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I did not produce a Bill of 1892 ; it was the report of that year. The Civil Service Act had been in force for many years and had been amended from time to time.

We will say, then, that the minister held up the Civil Service Report of 1892, and threatened this side that if we tried to show that the civil service at the present time was not up to the high standard he would like to lead the people to believe it to be he would quote from this report. But if the hon. gentleman will allow us to quote extensively from the recent report of the commissioners, we will show that, so far as the civil service is concerned it is degenerating rather than improving, and so far as the Earl of Duf-ferin was concerned, he was not finding fault with the civil service as it was in 1878. Lord Dufferin went on :
If you take my advice, you will never allow your civil service to be degraded into an instrument to subserve the ends and interests of any political party. The success of a political party ought to depend upon its public policy and the ability of its chief, and not upon the advantage likely to accrue to its individual adherents. In fact, the more the area of personal profit consequent upon a change of government is limited, the better for the country at large. On the other hand, the independence thus conceded to the members of the civil service imposes upon them a special obligation, namely, that they should serve their successive chiefs-no matter to which side they may belong-with a -scrupulously impartial zeal and loyalty. There is no offence which should be visited with swifter or more condign punishment than any failure in this respect. A civil servant who allows his political sympathies to damp his ardour, devotion, zeal and loyalty to his departmental chiefs is a disgrace to his profession.
These are strong words from the Earl of Dufferin. When we find men attempting, as some are, to burk inquiry into the civil service, we cannot but feel that the time has come when civil service reform becomes imperative.
Mr. Speaker, I draw your attention, once more, to the fact that the hon. gentleman (Mr. Armstrong) is reading his speech.	,

And I wish to call the attention of the hon. gentleman to a letter in my possession which will show that the patronage system is carried to its utmost, is carried on in most reckless fashion under the present government. I am sorry the hon. member for Halifax is not in his seat, because 1 have a letter here, and printed on top of it are the words ' M. Carney & Co., Halifax, N.S., February 19, 1906.'
Gordon Farnell, Esq.,
Dear Sir,-Your letter received. We recommend you to tender $1 below what Stewart has the contract for. We think he will be as high as before, maybe higher. Get the contract. Afterwards it may be in order to get more.
We are, dear sir,
Your obedient servants,

This goes to show the extent to which the patronage system is carried in Canada. When we see the present system carried to this extent it is high time that we should put forth our best energies to see that a civil service reform Bill is placed before this parliament with the least possible delay. There is not a doubt in my mind that as the Minister of Finance says that the ministers are responsible for what occurs in their departments, he will say that the Postmaster General is responsible for the letter that was printed by these men, possibly down in Halifax.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Certainly I say that the Postmaster General is not responsible for a letter which is not written by him, or by any of his officers.

I thought I understood the Finance Minister before dinner to say that the Postmaster General was responsible for the party patronage, and that the patronage committee were practically the source from which he gets his information. If this is a sample of the patronage committee that they have in the city of Halifax, and the way they are distributing the patronage in the different departments of this country, it is high time some investigation was made in regard to that system.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There is no reference there to the patronage committee, as the hon. gentleman quoted the letter. I did not hear anything in it about the patronage committee. I heard that the representatives from Halifax advised a man to tender low. There was nothing wrong in that. He said they might afterwards be able to get some more. I do not say that that was right, but the Postmaster General is not responsible for that. If the hon. gentleman can say that the contractor got anything more improperly, the Postmaster General would be answerable.
It is not wrong for a man to say that he would likely get more, and to tender $1 below the other man?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Not $1 below' the other man, but $1 below the existing contract price. That would be a perfectly legitimate advice to give, with the expectation of getting more. I wTould not write such a letter. Although I do not think any harm came of it, the Postmaster General could only be held responsible if he gave more.

I think I should read this letter again so that the Finance Minister may understand it fully.
Gordon Farnell, Esq.
Dear Sir,-We recommend you to tender $1 below what Stewart has the contract for. We think he will be as high as before, maybe higher. Get the contract. Afterwards-
This is the nice point.
-afterwards it unay be in order to get more.
We are, dear sir,
Your obedient servants,
Who are they ?
I understand they are the members for Halifax.
Did they get more?
I have not investigated that, perhaps the ex-Minister of Railways will look into the question for us and see if they did get more.
I would take your word for it.

It seems strange that they would make this promise that he should get more, if they did uot see that he did get more. However, I can only say that I strongly support the position taken by the hon. member for North Toronto. I think that members of parliament on both sides of the House are desirous of seeing a civil service reform Bill brought down that will not only be of benefit to the civil servants who are doing their duty in carrying out their contracts in a proper manner, but that will fill the public offices by men who are worthy of the position, and who will faithfully protect the public interest. Every dollar that these men are distributing through Canada belongs to the people of Canada, it does not belong to any government. Therefore I say that we should have the very best civil servants that this country can produce. I hope the resolution which is now before the House will obtain the support of members on both sides of the House.

If what has been read by my hon. friend (Mr. Armstrong) who has just taken his seat, is to be considered as orthodox,

while the platitudes he has expressed are of a very high altitude, I fear that I cannot be considered entirely orthodox. I think the same evil arises in politics that frequently arises in religions, because hypocrisy pervades every class of politician, as it pervades many of the religious classes in this world. Now, sir, it seems to me that we are dealing with a question of civil service reform. My hon. friend from Lambr ton closed his speech with a reference to the distribution of patronage. I understand civil service reform and patronage to be two entirely separate questions. It may be true that there are evils in connection with the civil service, it may be true that occasionally men who are not qualified are appointed to public offices. If that is true today, it has been true in Canada for the last 25 or 30 years, even before that time. But I think it can be fairly said in respect to the public service of Canada, that in the main it is filled by men of high character, men well qualified to fill the positions to which they are called, whether you refer to the inside or to the outside service. While it may be fashionable in a sense to declaim against this so-called evil, imaginary in the main, and while this criticism may be indulged in in a stereotyped way, yet to look at the question fairly from a practical standpoint, is there a man in this House or out of it who can say that the evil, in so far as it is an evil, would not exist after the institution of competitive examinations? I do not oppose that principle but in my judgment it will not cure the difficulty. There is influence and influence. Political influence is not the only influence that is exercised in connection with the appointment of men to office, and when we talk about competitive examinations, it seems to me that we do not reflect as to what those examinations are. I heard a reflection with respect to the appointment of postmasters, because, forsooth, they had not been called upon to pass an examination. What is the nature of an examination ? The young man from school is fitted perhaps to pass that examination, but I venture to say that if the members of this House were called upon to pass it, to answer the questions asked, nine-tenths of them could not do so, as they are so far removed from their school days. Would it be claimed that because they could not pass those examinations they are not fitted to fill positions such as that of postmaster ? My own experience and observation with respect to the civil service at Ottawa and elsewhere is that the young man who has been forced to work his way, who has been schooled by experience, who has had to battle with the ups and downs of life, and who seeks and secures a position in one of these departments is the man who in nine cases out of ten will fill the position with greater credit to himself and with Mr. EMMERSON.
greater satisfaction to the country than the university student who steps out from his college halls and can pass the examination. Can it be said that the answering of certain examination questions is a thorough test? Does it indicate qualifications of capacity, originality and initiative? The best civil servant is the man who has originality of thought, who can initiate an idea and carry it into execution, not the man whose memory is the best and who can answer questions, geographical, historical, mathematical or otherwise. Any hon. member who reflects will realize that it is not the man who graduates from college at the head of the honour class who makes the successful business man or the successful man in the real conflict of life. Very often the man who does not succeed in those examinations is, from a practical standpoint, the best man and scores the highest successes in the battle of life. So I hold that the competitive examination will not cure these evils.
There are influences apart from political influences. My hon. friend referred to my experience in connection with the Intercolonial and the Department of Railways and Canals. I can say in all honesty and seriousness that men were appointed and are being appointed to-day in connection with that railway because of their qualifications, because of their fitness. I will admit and I have admitted on the floor of this House that under existing conditions of party government in this country I, as a man, if it came to a question of selection between a political friend and a political opponent, other things being equal, would favour the political friend. Why? For the simple reason that I want a man who will work in concert and in sympathy with me. There is political influence in the service but it is not always political influence favourable to the party in power. There is as much political influence in the civil service in the departments at Ottawa to-day in favour of hon. friends opposite as there is against them. It will be admitted that such influence does not prevail on either side to any great extent, but in so far as civil servants indulge in their political convictions, in so far as they may be led to favour this or that side, the evil does not exist against the Conservative party to a greater extent than it does against the Liberal party. If our hon. friends opposite will but admit it, they know that they have as many friends politically in the civil service, not only at Ottawa but throughout the country, as have the Liberals. I am not confining my remarks to the inside civil service. I refer to the outside service as well. As to the Intercolonial, and I know the men of the Intercolonial as well as any man in Canada, there are more men in the service of that railway whose political prejudices are against the Liberal government than there are men politically in favour of it. Hon. friends opposite know it, and any one from

New Brunswick or who has knowledge of those employees will admit that to be the condition in that province and from end to end of the Intercolonial Railway.
My hon. friend from Lambton (Mr. Armstrong) assumed a very high altitude and delivered an essay very well in its way but certainly not practical. The essay was pleasant to listen to as he read it, but, Sir, we are dealing with practical things. During my political experience I have often listened to those who have favoured legislation with a view to reforming human nature. My experience has been that this cannot be done by legislative enactment, and I believe that if you base all your hopes upon making human nature different from what it is, from what you find it, by an attempt at legislation, failure will be written in large letters wherever that attempt is made.
How is it that other countries are able to accomplish these things ?

Other countries have not accomplished it. My hon. friend has referred to Great Britain and they have had civil service reform in Great Britain, but go to the departments of the public service there and see if you can find the evidence of it. Do the English civil servants who come to this country stand any higher in intellect, in capacity, in common sense, in initiative than our civil servants do ? I appeal to any one who has experience in this respect to say if he thinks the introduction of what is called civil service reform in Canada would bring the benefits which the hon. gentleman has dwelt on. I have some experience of the administration of affairs both federal and state in the United states and I can say that my experience is that the standard of the civil service in the United 'States is not as high as is the standard of the Canadian civil service. I say that the officials in the outside and inside service of Canada will more than favourably compare with similar officials in Great Britain or in the United States. It is true there has been a real attempt on the part of all governments to live up to our Civil Service Act, but it is also true that there has been failure and I will not agree that such failure has been a disaster to the counti'y. The success of the civil service in my opinion lies more in the common sense that is exercised in the selection of individuals to fill positions than it does in the administration of the Civil Service Act. I see gentlemen sitting on the opposite benches who I believe could not pass the civil service examination, but am I to be told that because of that they are not fitted to be post-masters or officers of the excise, or officers of the customs, or to fill various positions in the public service ? Is it to be said that a man who has had experience in the public affairs of this country, a man who knows the working of our constitutional system and a man who has knowledge of our business life is not fitted to fill a position of trust and responsibility simply because he cannot answer certain questions in mathematics or give the dates of historical happenings ? I fear we are carrying this idea too far. My hon. friend (Mr. Armstrong) told us that time and again during political contests, presidents of the United States have advocated civil service reform. That is a high sounding phrase and we have heard of it in this country as well as in the United States. I hold that men should be qualified for the offices to which they are appointed, but I also hold that the test of qualification is not to be found in an examination on set questions any more than is the capacity of a man who comes out of college to be measured by the examinations which he has successfully passed even if he be in the honour class. The school of experience best fits men for positions of trust and responsibility. When my hon. friend (Mr. Armstrong) spoke of the want of probity that has been found here and there among the thousands of civil servants, does he think that lack of probity would be removed by an educational test or a competitive examination ? Training and environment may be taken into consideration, but the answers a man may give to set questions on an examination paper will not alone qualify him from the standpoint of integrity and probity to fill a public position. Among the thousands of the employees of the government how few there are who fall in the way of temptation. Take the history of Canada since confederation, go into the postal service, the excise service, the customs service, go into every service of the government and see how few have fallen. The hon. gentleman spoke of the temptation that arises in connection with the distribution of patronage and incidentally he referred to the desix-e of men to get all they can from the government. That in a measure is true but after all it is human nature, and it is not alone in the political arena that such weakness is to be found. In the management of our charitable organizations, in the management of our church organizations if you like, human nature will be found to be equally weak. It is my opinion that the cant and hypocrisy that is indulged in in connection with this question is calculated to mislead the people of this country as to the practical working of our governmental system. As between the two great parties in Canada it would seem to me that honours are about easy in the sinning in connection with civil service appointments. During the eighteen years that hon. gentlemen opposite were in power I had an opportunity of observing their methods, and I can truly say they ignored all these principles which they now advocate for the civil service. My hon. friend from North Toronto has joined the army of latter day saints but he was a member of a government
91S3

*whose methods were not above reproach. When the Conservatives came to power in 1878 they dismissed nearly 500 employees from the Intercolonial, and they replaced them next day with their own partisans. Even a Civil Service Act would not have prevented these gentlemen from pursuing that course.
Take the men who were high in office in the Intercolonial in 1878. There was Air. Brydges, one of the most competent railway men who has ever been on this continent, and certainly one of the most efficient who has ever had a home in Canada. I will not say that he had to walk the plank; perhaps that is not a high sounding phrase; but his services were dispensed with. Hr. Lut-trel, who came from Ontario and went to the maritime provinces, was a railway man of capacity and efficiency, and he too was told that his services were no longer required. One after another of those in the employ of the Intercolonial at that time were obliged to step down and out, and their places were filled by partisan friends of lion, gentlemen opposite, and they continued for eighteen years to hold those positions. And where to-day are the men whom hon. gentleman opposite appointed in 1878? They are holding high positions in the railway service of Canada. The manager who was there when this government came into power in 1898 is there to-day, and almost every head official, every one who could give effect to his political prejudices quietly is allowed to remain. Would it have been any better if these men had been under a Civil Service Act? Does my hon. friend from Lambton propose to work out a system of civil service reform by which every official and employee of the Intercolonial shall be called on to pass a certain educational examination? Are they to be put through their p's and q's? Is it to be determined whether they -will properly dot their i's or cross their t's? There is an educational system on the Intercolonial. The men employed in the various branches of the service where technical skill is required have to pass examinations; the men who run the trains, the engineers, the firemen, the brakemen, the conductors, even the switchmen, are all required to submit to certain educational and other tests, physical as well as intellectual. My hon. friend, in the remarks which he chose to address to my humble self in reference to the period when I had the honour of presiding over the Department of Railways and Canals, said there were hundreds of partisans appointed to the Intercolonial Railway service without regard to fitness or qualification.
Oh, no.

If my hon. friend's remarks meant anything, they certainly meant that, because my hon. friend was making an argument in favour of the sub-Mr. EMMERSON.
mission of a civil service that would require these men to pass a civil service examination. I then innocently, and I thought mildly, suggested to my hon. friend that he was speaking without any knowledge of the facts-that he was simply drawing on his imagination; and I want to tell him that if he will better acquaint himself with the conditions that have prevailed on that railway for a number of years past, he will find that qualifications are the first essential when men are appointed to positions on the Intercolonial Railway. In what way would civil service reform affect conditions on the Intercolonial ? My hon. friend called attention to the examinations that have been held in the Public Accounts Committee, and there again he drew upon his imagination. Would the hon. gentleman have a civil service reform Act that would, include the foreman of dredge scows, or the inspectors and foremen appointed from one end of the Dominion to the other? Many of these men are employed temporarily. Many, it is true, are permanent; but they are continued as permanent in the departments because of their efficiency. If any one will speak from a knowledge of what is transpiring daily in the departments in Ottawa, and will tell the truth and the whole truth, he will be forced to admit this. I can speak with some knowledge in respect of the Department of Railways and Canals, and I want to say that in the main and on the average the employees in that department will compare favourably with those of any department of government in Canada or the United States. And with regard to the men on the Intercolonial Railway-I am referring now to the great army of employees who are entrusted with the management of our trains-our telegraphers, our conductors, our brakesmen, our locomotive engineers, our firemen, even the men who are entrusted with the duty of looking after the track, the section foremen and the section men-they are men who will compare favourably with the same number and the same class of men connected with any railway on this continent; and it seems to me that when hon. gentlemen seek to condemn and criticise in a sweeping manner the employees of the government, no matter-under what conditions they are serving the interests of this country, they are creating an impression that is false and should not go abroad. I referred a moment ago to the English civil service. I do not wish to condemn sweepingly the men who fill positions there: but I will say this, that from the opportunities for observation which have been mine, they do not stand higher, either in point of intellect, capacity or integrity. than men to be found among the same classes in Canada. I would illustrate it in this way. It is true that when we sent to South Africa the best of our brawn, we sent men who had not in many instances been trained in the colleges, who

had not even been trained in respect toj military edication. But when Paardeberg, occurred, who were the men who distinguished themselves? Were they the trained men who had been disciplined under the rules of the British military service or were they Canadians who had originality of thought, who initiated ideas, who could exercise the eye and the brain and the hand? That was the class of men who made the British arms victorious at Paardeberg. You can carry that illustration into this question and compare the civil service of Canada with that of Great Britain in the same way. Many of our civil servants have not been trained in university halls, but they have been trained in a harder and better school. Many of them had to start out from the farm and work very hard, and what schooling they could secure they got at the night school. They worked all day in order to take advantage of that night school. Today these men are the equals of any to be found in the civil service of the United States or Great Britain.
It seems to me that in uttering these sincere convictions, 'while I am not orthodox, while I am not indulging in the cant and hypocrisy apparently too prevalent throughout this aDd other lands-in uttering these sincere convictions I am but doing justice to the practical conditions which prevail in this country. My hon. friend from Lambton (Mr. Armstrong) read to us a lesson with respect to our duties as representatives of the people. Well, it occurs to me that our highest duty is to study the conditions in the country and provide for those conditions. I am not averse to a Civil Service Act, but if the key note of that Act is to be the passing of certain educational tests, which are simply a test of memory-if that is to be the standard, and that alone, then I shall not favour any such legislation, whether it comes from this or any other government. We should apply common sense to this question, and I think I can say this on behalf of those who have been charged with the responsibility of administering government departments from confederation down that- in so far as I have had personal knowledge of or acquaintance with the gentlemen who have held positions in successive governments-they applied in the main the proper and the best test when making appointments-and that is seeking a knowledge of the capacity and breadth and ability and integrity of the men who were looking for office. My hon. friend very much mistakes the routine of the lives of ministers if he thinks their time is taken up in selecting men for positions.
Some reference was made to the patronage committee. I rather like the term. I want to say in all frankness that I have in every section of the riding I have the honour to represent a patronage committee from whom I ask opinions, and when cer-292
tain positions are to be filled, I write to these men-who are men of capacity and integrity and I know will not mislead me-* and ask them about the capacity, qualifications and character of the applicants and their political proclivities as well. Because wherever responsibility is thrust on me, if I can get the necessary qualifications within the ranks of my own party I shall do it. And there is not an hon. member opposite who, if he is true to himself, will not say the same thing. They did it when they had office, and if this country should ever lie under the misfortune of being misgoverned by them, they will continue to do it. Let us be honest about these things. Let us not endeavour to deceive ourselves. We are certainly not deceiving the people. And in doing that, we are meeting the views of the great masses of the people throughout Canada. Why, it is an outgrowth of party government. The same thing occurs in Great Britain and the United States despite their Civil Service Acts, and in making these remarks I am not in any way reflecting upon these high and moral reflections of the Pecksnifflau type or these flights into a higher atmosphere attempted by our hon. friends.
Higher criticism.

Yes, this species of higher criticism indulged In by hon. gentlemen opposite, but never put into practice when they had the opportunity.
There is one thing I want to say before sitting down, and that is with reference to the remarks of the hon. member for Lamb-ton (Mr. Armstrong) regarding political influence in connection with the Intercolonial Railway. I have said before, and I repeat, that there are influences not always political but which move the great railway system of Canada and the United States. These influences are just as baneful if political influence is baneful-as the small amount of political influence exercised or attempted to be exercised in connection with the government railway system of Canada. I have said that political influence, in so far as it is exercised, is most Insignificant as compared with the community of influence which is exercised through the boards of trade, and the latter will be admitted as not political in its character. The Canadian Pacific Railway, the Grand Trunk Railway, the Canadian Northern and the other great railway systems of Canada are moved by influences which you may not term political, but which are to be found in all the avenues of our business life, our social life and our church life. All these influences must be recognized. They are to be found in the church synods, in the conferences, in the associations, in the conventions. And they are an incident of human nature. No Civil Service Act will remove them from being exercised, nor will



It change the human nature which is necessarily a part of our system.
It seems to me that this amendment might very properly have been dealt with on another occasion, and might better have come up in another form. Certainly, no good can result from it, for, while it speaks of the principle, it does not show in concrete form how that principle is to be applied, the details worked out in practice, or the abuses which are complained of remedied. When the Bill of which the government has given notice is placed before us it will be well for us to discuss its details, for we can see whether it is far-reaching or limited. But, holding the convictions I do, and holding them sincerely as I do, I could not refrain from giving utterance to them. I want the country, if I am wrong, to know that I am wrong. I want the country to know just where I stand in this matter, and I am not ashamed of the position I take in reference to it.

speakeroldname: Mr. GEO. W. FOWLER (Kings and Albert).
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have no doubt the country is intensely interested, X have no doubt it is waiting and watching with bated breath to know just the position the hon. member for Westmoreland (Mr. Emmerson) takes upon this important question. I am glad the hon. gentleman has at last taken the country into his confidence and told them what his position is. And I must congratulate him upon having proven to his own satisfaction, and, I think I may say, to that of the hon. gentleman beside him -judging from the applause with which his remarks were received-that education is a serious handicap to any gentleman who enters the civil service of this country. The hon. gentleman said in so many words that to be an honor graduate of a university absolutely and utterly unfitted a man fox-occupying a position in the civil service ; that the less he knew the better he was qualified for the position.

If my hon. friend will allow me, I made no such statement, nor did I use any language from which such an opinion could fairly or properly be inferred.
I was pointing out that educational qualifications or the examination by which they were proven were not the sole test.

With the hon. gentleman's usual misfortune, he has been unable to make clear to the members of this House just what he did mean, for, taking his words as they were uttered, and reasoning logically from the statement no other conclusion could be reached than that education was a real handicap to a man
No, no.

The Minister of Customs (Mr. Paterson) does not agree with that. And yet that hon. gentleman pounded his desk when the hon. member for Westmore-Mr. EMMERSON.
land made that statement. I assumed that that statement struck a responsive choi'd in the heart and intellect of the Minister of Customs.
He did not say that.

That is exactly what the hon. gentleman did say, and ' Hansard ' will prove it to-morrow. I cannot agree with the hon. gentleman on that point. I will admit this-that a man may be a graduate of a university, and still be a fool, if you will. The bare fact that he has a diploma from the univei-sity does not confer common sense upon him, and without common sense no man can be successful in any walk of life. But, to say that education is not necessary and to say that we should do away with all educational tests, is, to my mind, to utter an absolute absurdity. Why, my hon. friend from Westmoreland would turn back the clock altogether. Why are we in this country spending tremendous sums of money to endow our educational institutions if education is a handicap and if in any walk of life the less education a man has the better he is fitted for almost any position he may fill ? The hon. gentleman would have us conclude that the most successful members of our civil sei-vice, the gentlemen who gender the best return to the country for the salaries given them, are men who have least education. He would do away with educational tests altogether. Why ? Because, as he tells us, they are only a test of memory and therefore worthless. Would he have members of the civil service .without memory ? Is it not an advantage to a man in the service that he should have a good memory ? The hon. gentleman does not undex-stand, apparently, the accepted idea of the uses of education. He seems to think that education means simply a jumble of dates, mathematics and that sort of thing. He forgets that the idea of education is the-training of the intellect, the development of the mind. And how are you to know whether a man has that training or not unless you subject him to examination ? How is it in the case of men appointed to the care of technical matter on the Intercolonial, for instance ? They must pass examination, they must show diplomas to prove that they are capable of filling the positions to whicii they seek appointment. If a man looks for appointment as a mechanical engineer, he must have a certificate that he has had the training of a mechanical, engineer, or he will not be employed. I had almost ceased being surprised at any statement that the hon. gentleman (Mr. Emmerson) might make, but I must confess that I was surprised when I heard him speak as he has spoken with reference to this matter.
Now, while the civil service of Canada is a very creditable service in the main, I do not agree with my hon. friend, for I think it can be improved. I think there is room for

improvement everywhere, in point of fact. My hon. friend would say that we stand still in Canada. He compares the civil service in Great Britain with the civil service in Canada, greatly to the disadvantage of the former. He speaks of some members of the British civil service who have come out here. I do not know to whom he can refer. I have never met any of these dunderheads that he speaks of as belonging to the British civil service. The civil service of Great Britain has given to that country some of the brightest minds the world has ever known. It gave a Milner to South Africa, a Cromer to Egypt and a Hart to China. Why, I could occupy the time from now until morning giving a list of the great men of the civil service of Great Britain, if it were necessary to do so ; but it is not. The hon. gentleman spoke of the Intercolonial. That is a favourite topic of his. And the terms in which he spoke of it, and of the people employed upon it, has given me a contrary opinion to that which I formerly held with regard to one subject. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Emmerson) is going to be a candidate again. It has been rumoured that he would not be a candidate. I judge that he is making a bid for the vote down there. He states that a majority of the people engaged in the service of the road are of the Tory persuasion. Now, Sir, that is a statement on which I must take issue with the hon. gentleman, and any person who looks over the statistics in connection with the elections in the county of Westmoreland will know very well that that is not the case, and I want to say here now that if it were the case, the hon. gentleman would not be sitting in the seat he occupies to-night. The hon. gentleman is only elected by the votes of people employed in the shops at Moncton ; outside the city of Moncton the hon. gentleman does not and cannot get a majority.

I presume that my hon. friend wants to be accurate, therefore I may tell him that my majority outside the city of Moncton at the last election was some 300 or 400. My majority was between 1,000 and 1.100, and I only had a majority of between 600 and 700 in' the city of Moncton. Therefore I had some hundreds outside the city.

Well, I accept the hon. gentleman's statement. But I say that at the last local election the majority outside the city of Moncton was very much the other way, and I think the hon. gentleman, when he faces his electors again, will find that to be the case. The Conservative majority outside the city of Moncton was a very large one, and had it not been foil the vote of the railway shops, the four Conservative candidates would have been elected in that county. The hon. gentleman would have us think that all the old 2924
men who were appointed on the Intercolonial during the Conservative regime, in the city of Moncton, were continued, that no changes were made. He spoke of the changes that were made in 1878, and he cited two cases, I think Mr. Brydges and Mr. Luttreil. The hon. gentleman forgets that the chief engineer of the Intercolonial was dismissed after his party came into power.

After investigation, and for cause.
Mr. FOWLER, Yes, for cause, because he obeyed the order of his superior. Now the hon. gentleman also denies most strenuously that there were strained relations between himself and the then Minister of Railways, because he would not accede to his attempts to secure the dismissal of the present manager of the railway.
That statement is very far from the facts, nothing ever transpired in that direction at all. My relations with Mr. Blair were in no way affected by reason of that.

I can only say that it was very current at the time and that the statement came from his close friends and relatives, just as close blood relatives as you can get. I suppose the hon. gentleman will also deny that there were strained relations between himself and Mr. Blair.

No, our relations were almost of the most friendly character. Mr. Blair and I-if this is pertinent and relative to this discussion-were always the closest personal friends. He thought differently on some political matters, but not in connection with the officials of the Intercolonial.

So far as that is concerned, we must accept the statement of the hon. gentleman, no matter how much we know to the contrary. Now, Sir, this is not the first time that matter was referred to. Mr. Blair was at that time alive, and -was in this House, and I myself had the honour to refer to it, and the hon member for Westmoreland (Mr. Emmerson) did not then deny, because Mr. Blair was here, I suppose that was the reason that Mr. Emmerson would not deny it.
If he were here and heard my hon. friend's statement he would deny it, because it is not in accord with the truth.

My hon. friend was here, and the scene that took place between the two gentlemen, the scene of reconciliation, was most pathetic, when the hon. gentleman as I stated then, fell upon the neck of Mr. Blair and admitted that he had sinned -that is, that Mr. Blair had sinned-and Mr. Blair admitted that he had sinned and

was willing to be forgiven. Tliat is^ within the memory of hon. gentlemen in thi>s House; and then my hon. friend did not get up and deny it, as he has denied it tonight.
Now, Sir, so far as civil service reform is concerned, I think this resolution is certainly along the line of improvement. It does not seem to me that it is the correct thing for us to stand in the way of this improvement. What argument has been put forward against this resolution? The sole argument of the Finance Minister to-day was, you were in power for 18 years, you had a civil service reform report made in 1892, and nothing was done under it. That is the sole argument. Is there to be no advance in this country? Is there to be no improvement. Twelve years have elapsed since our hon. friend's opposite came into power, they have had the advantage of that 1892 report, because it was not a report to the Conservative party but to the government of Canada; they are now the government of Canada, and that report has been before them. Therefore if the Conservative government, if the Conservative party, who were in power in 1892 were remiss in their duty in not acting upon that report up to 1896, four years, how much more reprehensible has been the conduct of this government who have been in power 12 years, three times as long, and have still delayed acting upon it. Therefore they are threefold as guilty as the old government.
I listened to the speech of the hon. member for North Toronto, I think his speech was absolutely non-partisan in its tone, and high in its character. How was it met by hon. gentlemen who spoke from the other side? With sneers, that is all. My hon. friend from East Lambton (Mr. Armstrong) spoke of the high character which the civil service should maintain, spoke along the lines of obtaining for the civil service the highest possible character in the men who are appointed, and in the promotion that would be thrown around those men, yet my hon. friend from Westmoreland (Mr. Emmers'on) has answered that with a sneer. He drags in the church, as the hon. gentleman always does when he speaks. Surely that is not very high statesmanship on the part of our friends opposite. Surely if they are going to persist in their present line, if they are going to retain the civil service as it is at present, and the civil service system as it is at present, surely they have some better defence for it than sneering against the propositions of hon. gentlemen on this side of the House. I would think that we have a right to expect from the government that is in charge of the affairs of this country a very different line of argument.
Now what do we desire to do? What does the hon. member for North Toronto, by his resolution, desire to do? He desires to remove as far as possible the civil ser-Mr. FOWLER.
vice of Canada from the influence of politics so that merit should be the only thing to be recognized. What to-day is the only thing recognized? Is it merit? No, it is political pull. That is the way promotions are made, not by merit but by political pull. So much the better for the country if it sometimes happensi, as I have no doubt it does happen, that political pull and merit happen to be united in the same person. But there is many a man in the civil service to-day, meritorious, thoroughly equipped, able in every way, yet he gets no advancement by reason of the fact that he is suspected of being sympathetic towards the party that is now, and will be for a week or two yet, in opposition in this country-only for a brief time, however, I may say, for the benefit of my hon. friends opposite. Now what we propose is to remove that political influence with respect to promotions in the civil service of this country; what we propose is to throw a protection around the civil servants of this country so that they may no longer, if they wish to speak on political subjects to a friend, whisper it where no one can hear; so that they may be able to vote as their conscience dictates without having to watch to see if anybody is trying to find out how they vote, if that vote happens to be cast against the party in pow7er. Because I hold that the civil servant in this country has just as much right to exercise his franchise as has the member of this House, he has an absolute right to vote either for or against the party in power. I do not believe that he should go upon the public platform and advocate the principles of either party; if he does that, if he goes that far, he must fall with his party and should resign when his party goes out of power.
Does not the right to vote carry with it the right to use legitimate influence for a principle ?

Logically that may be correct, but it would open the door to a great many difficulties that must be avoided by simply allowing the civil servant the right to vote and to express his opinions, not on the public platform and not taking an active part as a canvasser. There seems to be a distinction there, even although my hon. friend does not seem able to perceive it.

I am following this debate. I have heard that statement by different speakers, but I have not heard a good reason why it should not be done. If this government employ men and forbid them to use legitimate influence in favour of principles that they consider good for this country, would it not be just as reasonable for employers of labour to forbid men who happen to work for them to ex-
