press opinions because those happened to be against their own ? Mr. FOWLER. No employer of labour would permit his employee to go out and become an active canvasser on behalf of the rival institution over the way. Mr. R. SMITH. In England it is a common thing to find men on the public platform with their employer advocating opposite political principles. Mr. FOWLER. There is no objection to their advocating different political principles, but I say if the employee of one manufacturing concern was advocating the advantages of the opposition manufacturing concern over the way, he would not hold his employment very long and that seems to me to be a fair illustration of the position in so far as the civil service is concerned. I have nothing further to add, I have simply to say that I believe the resolution of the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster) is along the right lines and is a resolution which every man should feel himself able to support. I think the government should adopt it. It is not necessarily a vote of want of confidence. The government can consider it not a vote of want of confidence and the whole House can vote for it. Let us try to improve the conditions of the civil service if we can, let us improve the conditions of the civil servants in every way in which it is necessary to make improvements. If we are not paying enough let us pay more ; let us be sure, however, before we increase the salaries of the civil servants, that the salaries are not large enough now. Mr. R. L. BORDEN (Carleton, Ont.). As no hon. gentleman on the opposite side of the House seems disposed to continue the debate, I would like to say a very few words before it closes. The hon. member for Westmoreland (Mr. Emmerson) treated the House to a very frank declaration of the stand which he takes on this subject, but let me say that if he did touch and I do not think he very closely touched the real question, everything that he said and fifty times more, was answered in Great Britain more than half a century ago by men like Mr. Gladstone and Lord Macaulay, whose utterances on this subject would most completely dispose of every possible argument that has been advanced to-night by the hon. member for Westmoreland and would dispose also of a great many more formidable arguments which he did not advance. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) has dealt in the first place with the time at which my hon. friend for North Toronto (Mr. Foster) has brought this subject forward. He did not allude to the fact that this motion was placed on the order paper	on the very first day of this session, that its consideration was postponed from time to time for the purpose of having before , the House the report of the Civil Service Commission, and finally when that report did not come down until the government had taken practically every day for their own business the hon. member for North Toronto dropped his motion from the order paper with a distinct statement that he would renew it after the report of that Commission was available to members of . this House. Therefore, so far as the question of time is concerned, there is nothing with which to reproach the member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster). The Minister of Finance also relied upon the claim that this was a motion of want of confidence in the government, being a motion in amendment of that proposed by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) that the House should resolve itself into Committee of Supply. The hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster) did not put this forward as a motion of want of confidence in the government; he deliberately abstained from introducing matters of a controversial nature except in reply to some observations made during his speech by the hon. Minister of Customs (Mr. Paterson) and even then he touched the matter with a very light hand and his speech, on the whole, might he said to be of an absolutely uncontroversial nature. Over and over again this government, since it came into power in 1896, has accepted amendments proposed in a very much more controversial spirit and they have passed, in some cases by a majority and in most cases by the unanimous consent of this House. In 1899 Sir Charles Tupper proposed a resolution as an amendment to the motion for Committee of Supply, touching the responsibility of political heads of departments. The government accepted the motion and it passed the House unanimously. In 1900, Mr. Russell, then member for the City and County of Halifax, proposed a resolution with regard to preferential trade with Great Britain. The motion was accepted by the government and passed by a majority. In 1901, Mr. T. O. Davis, then a member of this House, proposed a motion with regard to the test case touching the taxation of Canadian Pacific lands in the west. The government accepted the motion and it passed unanimously. In 1902, Mr. Bourassa proposed an amendment with regard to the embargo imposed by Great Britain on Canadian cattle. It was accepted by the government and passed this House unanimously. In 1903, Mr. Costigan, then a member of this House, proposed an amendment with regard to the question of Home Rule for Ireland. The government accepted the amendment and it passed by a majority. In 1905, Mr. Armstrong, the member for

East Lambton, proposed a resolution in amendment for an efficient system of cold storage. The government accepted the amendment and it passed unanimously. In 1905 the member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Lake) proposed a resolution with respect to the interference of civil servants in Dominion and provincial elections. The government accepted the amendment and it passed unanimously. All these rt'ere amendments to the motion for Committee of Supply. During this very session, I myself proposed a resolution in this House in amendment to supply .touching the rights of parliament to original documents in possession of departments of the government. I did not take the course which the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster) has taken to-day ; I proposed that resolution in a very controversial spirit indeed and challenged the government to vote it down if they dared. They accepted the motion and it passed this House unanimously. It is idle then for the government to pretend that they must reject this motion to-day on the ground that it is an amendment to the motion for Committee of Supply.
The Minister of Finance dwelt very lightly on the subject of civil service reform and he and the member for Westmoreland (Mr. Emmerson) justified appointments to the civil service of Canada by means of patronage committees in the different constituencies. They qualified the real object of patronage committees by suggesting that it is to afford to the government or to the head of a particular department information as to who mav be the best man available. But every 'one who knows the real object of' the patronage committee knows that such is not the purpose for which it is formed, nor the motive which actuates its work. Nine times out of ten what influences the patronage committees is not whether a particular man is the best man for the public service, but whether the amount of party service he has performed entitles him to the position. The question debated above all others in the patronage committee is whether or not a particular appointment will do the party the most good in the particular district from which the man is appointed. My hon. friend (Mr. Emmerson) spoke a great deal about hyprocrisy in religion and politics and I shall not follow him in that, but I do say that if he has the slightest knowledge of these patronage committees, he will understand that I have correctly described their purpose and motive. Is it advisable in Canada to continue the system of making appointments to the public service through the instrumentality of the political organizations of one party or the other ? If it is a good system, as the Minister of Finance and the member for Westmoreland seem to think, then why not allow the patronage committees to recommend promotions in the service, why not refer the question of Mr. R. l. BORDEN.
promotion to the patronage committee of the particular district from which the appointee in the first instance came. If you analyze the suggestion in that way you will see how utterly absurd and misleading it is to say that any such system can be in the interest of this country or any other country possessing self-governing institutions.
My hon. friend from North Toronto has made a very able and exhaustive speech in support of his motion and so I shall not deal with the question at any great length. Let me quote the words of a well known writer in the United States which expressed very distinctly and very forcibly the maxim that public office is a public trust. I take this citation from a pamphlet written by Wm. Dudley Foulke, a member of the National Civil Service Reform League of the United States:
Public office being a trust, the man or party who administers it has no more right to bestow it for personal gratification or political advantage than a judge would have to take away the property of a litigant on personal or party grounds. If it is asked then, why we want appointments controlled by rules and examinations, why we are not willing to trust the discretion of the executive or that of the legislators by whom the executive functions are now so largely assisted, we answer: For the same reason that we insist that the judge who passes on our lives, liberty or property, shall be governed by fixed rules of law.
My hon. friend from Westmoreland was very strong in liis contention that we should apply common sense; let me quote from the present Attorney General of the United States, who has made a careful study of this subject :
I want to tell you then, in a very few words, what civil service reform is. It is nothing in the world, ladies and gentlemen, but the application of sound sense and sound morals to the choice and retention of your public servants. You place in the hands of a president, or a mayor, or a governor great powers of pat' ronage. He holds those powers, he is entitled to fill the offices in his gift, solely in the public interest. He received those offices, or the right to fill .them, from the people; he did not create them. The salaries of those officers are paid by the people's money; they are not paid out of his pocket. The duties of those officers are fixed by the people's laws; he has no more power than any other citizen to fix their duties, although he himself is hound, by the same laws, to see that those duties are properly performed. In short, the offices in his gift belong to the people, and he holds them as the people's steward and trustee.
And as to the history and objects of civil service reform perhaps I cannot do better than to quote the Hon. Carl Shurz. a man of international reputation :
The reform of the civil service as we advocate it, aims at two objects: to secure to the people an honest and efficient public service, and to eliminate as much as possible the demoralizing element of patronage and political and personal favouritism from out political

life. The first is accomplished by subjecting candidates for public employment to examinations and probations testing their fitness for such employment; -and the second by making such examinations competitive, so as to give the fittest man the best chance for appointment and to exclude appointment by favouritism, personal or political, and thus the use of the office concerned -as party spoil. This is not a matter of abstract theory, but of simply practical common sense.
I do not know that I can add much to tbe arguments in favour of civil service reform *which are contained in these three citations. Let me ask what will he accomplished by civil service reform ? In the first place we will accomplish better service to the state. No one pretends, as my hon. friend from Westmoreland, seemed to think we pretend that appointment by competitive examination will in every case bring the best man into the proper place. I do not believe competitive examination will accomplish that, but I do believe that by that system you will get an infinitely better class of officials than you will get by the exercise of mere party patronage and mere political pull. In the next place you will bring about a more assured status for the civil servant, and it is important that the civil servant should have ail assured status. The man who understands that the exercise of political influence can put over his head in the government service another man who upon a fair test of merit would never get the position, will surely not feel himself inspired with the same interest in the public service as if he knew that faithful and intelligent work done by him would in time bring about its fitting reward. In the next place it will remove the power and therefore the temptation to appoint to public office for personal or party ends. I do not know any distinction between bribing a man by money and bribing a man by the promise of public office, and when you have a system under which any man engaging in political work feels himself assured at some time in the future of obtaining a public office because of the mere fact that he has done that political work, you do not get very far away from bribery. In tbe third place, the reform which my hon. friend from North Toronto is advocating will strike down that political corruption which does more or less arise from the use of party patronage.
The present system causes many and various abuses to flourish. In the first place, the heads of departments do not appoint their subordinates. In some cases at least subordinates in the different departments are appointed when they are not required. The head of the department would not select the man whom he is bound to receive if he were left to exercise his own good judgment. Inefficient appointments are made. There are useless men in the departments in Ottawa to-day ; every
minister of the Crown knows that. I do not mean to say that the men now on the treasury benches are responsible for all of them. I am not making this statement with any idea of casting discredit on the government. The same system as has flourished under this government, perhaps in the more intense degree, has also flourished under the previous administration. Under both. I believe, not only have inefficient appointments been made hut places have been created in order that political supporters of one party or the other might be satisfied in their demands. The political influence of appointees is exercised. That more or less destroys discipline. My hon. friend from Westmoreland (Mr. Emmerson)-who has left the chamber, I regret to say-spoke of the Intercolonial railway and the marvellous condition of affairs under his administration. I have been told, on authority which I respect as highly as I do that of the hon. member for Westmoreland, that there are men on the Intercolonial today who cannot and dare not keep their subordinates under them in a proper system of discipline simply because they know the effect which the political influence of these subordinates, appointed by political pull, can exercise upon them. Does that tend to good service or good discipline ? Political support is bartered for promise of office, and the time of ministers and members is needlessly and absurdly taken up with patronage. My hon. friend from Westmoreland was rather inclined to deny that.
I have discussed this subject with hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House who are sincerely desirous of seeing reform in this connection brought about. I have not discussed it with ministers, and do not know what their experience may be ; but members of parliament on the other side of the House have told me, in some cases that half their time, in other cases that three-fourths of their time, was taken up in dealing with matters of appointment to public office, and in that way they were prevented from giving that attention to public affairs that they would like to give and that they would be able to give if this system were abolished and a system of competitive examinations were substituted for it. In the United -States, according to the pamphlets to which I have just referred, the abuse previous to the inaugura tion of their present system, existed to an enormous extent. One of the writers whom I have quoted describes a visit which he made to one of the departments at Washington, where -he found a regular book like a ledger kept in which every member of Congress and every senator was not only with every appointment which had been made upon his recommendation, but -with the salary and position described, so that it might be known exactly by a

glance at this book from time to time, to what extent his power of recommendation to office had been exercised. It reached a ridiculous extent in the United 'States, such an extent as influenced public opinion, and brougnt about the establishment of the National Civil Service Reform League, and created such a public agitation that civil service reform has made enormous progress in that country. While they may not yet have attained the standard that has been attained in Great Britain, no one can deny, notwithstanding the vain remarks of my hon. friend from Westmoreland, that their system is many years in advance of that which we have in Canada. It is idle to pretend that the civil service of Canada, under a system of party patronage, is equal or can be equal to that of Great Britain. The civil service system of Great Britain is the admiration of the world, and when any hon. gentleman arises in this House and declares that our system is equal to or at all approaching it, he merely shows that he has made no study whatever of the subject, and does not in the least know that which he professes to discuss. I do not deny that we have splendid civil servants in Canada ; but their value is great, not by reason of our system, but in spite of.it. It may sometimes happen, it does very often happen, that an appointment made for political reasons is a very good appointment, and the man so appointed may render excellent service to the state. But we must not on that account shut our eyes to the abuses that have arisen, and to the general demoralization in the public life of the country when the reward of office is regarded as a fair exercise of the party power. If a party continues in power, as it very often does, for eight or ten or twelve years, even for eighteen years, as in the case of one administration, the result is that the appointments, made almost altogether from one political party, leave a large minority in the country absolutely unrepresented in the public service. In other words, you exclude from the civil service of the country the ability, the capacity, the good character,. of nearly one-half the population, who, by reason of this system of party patronage, are not considered as eligible for appointment to the public service. Is it not time that we in Canada should do away with that system ? Suppose any great banking institution in Canada, any great railway corporation, any great commercial corporation, made appointments to their service from political considerations or the equivalent of political considerations, do you imagine that it would have the splendid service which many of these great organizations possess 1 And is there any reason why the government of this country, which ought to be the greatest and most efficient organization in Canada, should not have I Mr. R, L. BORDEN.
the very best and most efficient service that is to be found in Canada from the Atlantic to the Pacific ? Surely there is no reason why it should not be so. The public service presents certain attractions, and men are ready to enter it. If it were put on a reasonable, business, common sense basis, I cannot bring myself to think that it would not attain the same standard as has been attained in Great Britain, and that we should not have vastly improved results to the people of the country as a whole. I am glad to know, if I am properly advised, that the province of British Columbia in the present year is leading the way in establishing a system of open competitive examinations by a non-partisan board, and that in connection with the system which they are so establishing, they are making efficient provision for the old age of public servants of that province by proper superannuation allowances. We have this example. We have the example of all our business institutions throughout the country so far as superannuation is concerned. I agree with my hon. friend from North Toronto (Hon. Mr. Foster) that the two should go hand in hand. We want in Canada a system of appointment by competitive examinations, to be under the control of a board which shall give to that subject the whole of its time and energies, and endeavour to bring about in Canada the same conditions which have prevailed so many years in the mother country. That alone will not be sufficient. We have to put our civil service on a proper basis of remuneration and in the possession of the assurance that when old age comes, after reasonable service to their country, they shall not be turned out with the fear of poverty and distress before their, eyes, and that they and those dependent upon them shall be provided for by that same country which they have served for years.
My hon. friend from North Toronto (Mr. Foster) has proposed this resolution in no controversial spirit. He has proposed it as a motion which he thinks might reasonably be accepted by the government and which ought to be embodied in the measure they propose to submit to the House before many days. I sincerely trust the government will reconsider the attitude of my hon. friend the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) and thus take a great step forward in the progress towards civil service reform. We can all unite in the declaration of this principle-a principle which is not a new one, which is not an experimental one, which has been tried and tried successfully, in the mother country for half a century at least and which, during the past ten or fifteen years, has met with the same success in the great republic to the south.

Under ordinary cireum-

stances, I would have no fault to find whatever with the motion moved by my hon. friend from North Toronto (Mr. Foster). 1 may say to him at once that, in the principle laid down, I am disposed to very largely agree, if not absolutely. But in my humble judgment, the time is singularly ill chosen to present such a motion. -My hon. friend had many opportunities in the earlier part of the session to move this resolution. You, Mr. Speaker, had hardly taken your seat, when the hon. gentleman put on the notice paper the motion now in your hand. It was called again and again, he had every opportunity to move it, he did not do so for reasons better known to himself, he withdrew it at last in order to bring it on now as an amendment to the motion to go into Supply. But I would call attention to the fact that this very day, were it not for an unfortunate event which we all deplore, my hon. friend the Minister of Agriculture {Mr. Fisher) would in all probability have introduced a measure of civil service reform. It is not for me to say at the moment what will be the character of thajt measure; but when such a Bill was on the order paper, and when the cause why it was not brought before the House is known to my hon. friend, I would have expected that he would have waited until the Minister of Agriculture introduced his Bill. Then if the Bill were not to his taste, he could move his present motion by way of amendment or move it as an amendment on going into Supply. This is the only reason why we cannot accept the motion of my hon. friend. I am not discussing the merits of the Bill. If the rules of the House had permitted an amendment, I would have moved one which would have explained our position, but since we cannot explain our position by a motion, it isopen for us to explain it by giving our reasons against the motion. We do not want to enter into a controversy on the merit of my hon. friend's motion. We shall have every opportunity to do this when the government Bill comes up, as it certainly will in a few days, if not to-morrow.
This would be a sufficient answer at present, but in courtesy to my hon. friend perhaps I may notice some of the arguments he has offered to the House. Bet me say, first of all, that I do not want in this matter that we should appear better than our fellows. We have, in the twelve years we have been in office, accepted the system, which has been in existence since confederation, of making appointments on party lines. In this we followed the example set by all our predecessors. In the eighteen years the party opposite held office, appointments to the service were made on party lines also. It is said by my hon. friend that this system is not the best. I agree altogether with him, but even if the service has been recruited on party lines, I think it only fab- to say that the present service
is a very efficient body of men. For eighteen years it was recruited from the ranks of the Conservative party, yet on the whole I am satisfied that the great majority of the members, whether appointed through Conservative or Liberal influence, have ceased to be partisans, and while retaining their own convictions, they are, in the discharge of their duties, nothing but public servants. That recalls to me a conversation I had, shortly after taking office, with an eminent member of the service. He said to me: Of course I would not deny my convictions to you. I was appointed by the late government, but is it unnatural that I should act towards the government as honestly as I can ? Lawyers are all party men, but when a lawyer gives his services to a client, he does not know the politics of his client. In the same manner a public servant does not know the politics of the goveimment which employs him. But allowing this to be the case, I am not blind to the inconvenience and the condition of the service as it is today. There is a great deal in favour of a system of having appointments made simply on merits and not from other considerations. My hon. friend from North Toronto (Mr. Foster) has given the history of the service in other countries. He has stated truly that whilst in the beginning the civil service was recruited by every government from the ranks of the party in power, abuses crept in which induced first one government and then another to adopt the system advocated by my hon. friend from North Toronto (Mr. Foster). The British government led the way, the American government accepted the same principle, but I would observe to my hon. friend the leader of the opposition and the hon. member for North Toronto that it is a task of some difficulty to establish that system in a country like the United States. The first law adopted by congress goes back twenty-five years, if not more and then, after twenty-five years, it is not as much in force as it is in Great Britain.
That indicates we should lose no time.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
It indicates that we should lose no time. I quite agree with that. But we are ready. We have a notice of a Bill on the Order Paper, certainly we cannot go faster than that. And if we are to lose no time, my hon. friend should have told the hon. member (Mr. Foster), who sits next to him, because he has taken a good deal of time. He had his motion prepared six months ago, but it is only to-day that he has presented it to the House. We shall have, I hope, more diligence. But there is one thing we should do for the civil service. My hon. friend from North Toronto has spoken lengthdy and well upon the great benefit the civil service has rendered to the public. He has stated-In words not too strong for me

-the great advantage that a country like Canada derives from a good civil service. But perhaps he will agree that there is one duty that we owe to the civil service, a primary duty above all others that we should never forget. And it is very press-ing-we should pay them promptly the money that is due for their diligent service.

I am a little disappointed that the Prime Minister (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) did not see lit to deal with this question at an earlier period in the debate. However, he is an old parliamentarian and he perhaps knows best the time to take the matter up. "We have had complaint and excuse by both the First Minister and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) that the time is inopportune for dealing with this question. I have listened carefully to their arguments, but I have not been convinced; I have not been able to see that the time is inopportune. It would seem to me, with all deference to their opinion, that no more opportune time could possibly have been selected than now when we are about to discuss a Bill and before that Bill has been actually introduced. We know how difficult it is for the government to preserve its face after it has actually introduced a Bill, how difficult it is for them to come down from a position they have taken on the formal introduction of a Bill, and, therefore, how desirable it is that before they commit themselves to any scheme we should have a full discussion of the subject in parliament. Especially is this true with regard to this matter.
Now, the Prime Minister complains of the delay of the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster). He says that, almost before the Speaker has taken the Chair at the opening of the session, the hon. gentleman had given notice of a motion along these lines. So he did. Does the Prime Minister complain that he has had too timely a notice of this discussion? Let me say that, whilst I appreciate as a member of the House the fact that we have had ample notice so that we could take this matter into our careful consideration, I want to call attention also to the fact that he is hardly fair when, in dealing with the matter, he omits to mention that the hon. member for North Toronto was prevented from early and timely discussion of this question by the fact that the Civil Service Commission's report had not been brought down. And when the report was brought down the opportunity had gone by for dealing with this as a formal notice of motion. What does it propose ?
That the civil service system of Canada should be based on merit and character alone

Does the Prime Minister object to that? Does he think the civil service system of
Sir WILFRID LAURIER
Canada should not be based on merit or character, but should be, as it has been in the past, a subject of patronage, a subject regulated and controlled by politics as in the past, as admitted by every honest member of the House? This existed to some degree under former administrations, but it exists to a most dangerous and humiliating degree under the present administration. The discussion of this question, so far, has been very moderate-too moderate, I think, taking the attitude of hon. gentlemen who have spoken on the other side into consideration. I think it is no harm, probably to remind the Prime Minister that the country has become aroused to the position, particularly since the report of the Civil Service Commission which is studded with statements of the evils of the patronage system, and is aroused to the determination that the element of patronage and political interference shall be eliminated from the public service. The resolution goes on :
-and the appointments thereto should be made only from candidates whose competency has been established through open competitive examinations conducted under a non-partisan civil service commission.
Do hon. members object to that? Would they say that candidates should not be appointed by reason of competency? Do they claim that it is improper that competency be established by open competitive examination conducted under a non-partisan Civil Service Commission? Now, it seems to me that the only controversial point in this is the Civil Service Commission. There is not an lion, member on the other side who will join with the government in voting down this resolution who would dare to go to his constituents and say that he is opposed to any principle enunciated in that resolution unless it be by possibility the provision for a Civil Service Commission. That may or may not be a desirable solution of the question. But we have the example of other countries, notably Great Britain and the United States, in support of the principle of a Civil Service Commission of a nonpartisan character conducting these examinations. While the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance oppose this amendment they shoxv no reason except-and I say it advisedly because the right hon. Prime Minister has used this language- the quibbling reason, that the motion is brought at an inopportune time and even that reason is opposed by every fact connected wTith this matter. I say that hon. members who support the government are called upon to vote down this resolution upon reasons which will not commend themselves to the public. Let me examine some of the statements made in this connection by the Minister of Finance. And,
I must say, in passing, that I never saw that hon. gentleman (Mr. Fielding) more

embarrassed, more agitated, I might almost say more confounded, than he was this afternoon. And what is the reason? The right hon. gentleman who leads the House could give the answer, perhaps, if he saw fit. But the fact remains that the minister spoke for fifteen minutes without giving one substantial reason why this amendment should not be concurred in. The leader of the opposition has put it beyond question that the government is not bound to take the attitude that they have to vote against this amendment as a motion of want of confidence. My hon. friend the leader of the opposition has shown that not only in cases where a motion was brought forward that was not controversial in a party sense, but even where it was put forward in a controversial sense, and the government were challenged to vote it down, as in the case of the production of documents, they accepted the motion. What is their position to-night ? They ask their followers from one end of Canada to the other to vote down this proposition, and if they do so, perhaps nine-tenths of their followers will find it very embarrassing to them when they come to seek election within probably a very short period.
Now the Minister of Finance said that almost every one of the evils referred to by the hon. member for North Toronto existed under previous governments, and were mentioned by the previous commission. It may be so, but I have never found it in the report of the commission of 1892. It is noticeable that the hon. gentlemen who say so do not venture to give quotations from that report. But did not these hon. gentlemen say they were going to do better than the Conservatives ? Have they fulfilled their promises yet? The people do not think so. It was their duty to take up the report of that commission when they came into office and deal with it, but although eleven years have passed since then, they have done nothing towards reforming the abuses pointed out in the civil service system. Now the Minister of Finance says that the hon. member for North Toronto complained of the increases that were made from time to time as having been made on a political basis. I did not so understand my hon. friend from North Toronto. I rather think that the Minister of Finance felt guilty in that regard, and that he imagined something had been said that was not said. If the hon. member for North Toronto did not say it he could have said it. Any one who has watched the discussions in this House, as I have for eight years, knows perfectly well that when we have asked in reference to these increases the conclusion was irresistible, from the specious explanations given, that many of these increases had been made for political reasons alone, and a good many were denied their statutory increases where there could be no substantial reason given. The Minister of Finance
attempted to answer the complaint of the Royal Commission regarding the virtual amendment of the Civil Service Act by the introduction of the words ' notwithstanding anything in the Civil Service Act.' That has been an abuse during all the time I have been in the House, and it is growing yet. It is almost always inexcusable. An extraordinary attitude was taken by the Minister of Finance, I might almost say a damnable attitude, when he said that the evil of political influence was magnified. Mr. Speaker, it is scarcely possible to magnify the evil of this pernicious system of political influence, and political patronage. You cannot confine it, as the Minister of Finance suggested, to mere patronage committee alone, it is the patronage of the politician from one end of the country to the other, in regal'd both to the inside and the outside service, and the employees of the government who are not in the civil service, as well. Take up the report of the commissioners. Almost on every page of their report they speak about the influence of politics. On page 23 they say :
Owing to the good times which have recently been prevalent and the large revenues received from customs, the old-fashioned notions of frugality and liying within one's means have to some extent been departed from, and instances have been found of departments giving orders for stores and other services to he delivered within a year in excess of the vote granted by parliament. Large amounts have been spent at several places in the Dominion for supplies bought from those enjoying political patronage at what may be called retail rates.	[DOT]
I said a moment ago that it is not patronage committees only that we complain of but it is patronage lists that exist wherever stores or supplies of any kind are bought. Almost every official that was examined before the Royal Commission spoke of these lists as a matter of course, that of course everything was bought with a view to politics, that no service was performed, uo pei-son was employed, no goods were purchased, as a rule, except iu view of some political advantage to the party.
As a rule your commissioners found in the outside service that polities enter into every appointment, and politicians on the spot interest themselves not only in the appointments but in subsequent promotions of officers.
My bon. friend the leader of the opposition said, to follow out the argument of the hon. the Minister of Finance, that not only would you dictate the appointment but you would regulate the promotion afterwards. The commissioners have found that not only is the appointment controlled by the politician in the first instance, but the promotion. the status the man shall occupy from time to time, his progress, is guided by the band of the politician.

In the outside service those who have the ' political pull ' use it for all it is worth; they pass hy their superior officers and bring pressure to procure anything that may prove to their advantage.
Again-and this is in the Customs Department, I am sorry the Minister of Customs is not here:
The chief positions in the outside service of this department are political appointments. Every collector of customs has been appointed from the ranks of the party in power at the moment.
Again in the Inland Revenue Department:
Of course in the Inland Revenue Department political appointments to the public service prevail, and as a rule the officers in one distract are confined to that one district.
A great deal has been said about that district business, particularly on the Intercolonial Railway and services of that kind.
Is my hon. friend reading from the report about the Intercolonial Railway or is that just put in by my hon. friend himself?

That is a remark of my own, but in order to be altogether within the book I shall give some references to the Intercolonial Railway. I read now from the evidence of Mr. Butler on page 1185. He is asked :
Q- Most of the copyists are women?-A. Yes.
Q. Did politics have anything to do with their entering the service, do you know?-A. I imagine that influence was exerted in their favour; I imagine that political influence insured their appointment.
Q. But except in the case of one man you had nothing to do with it?-A. No.
Q. Nine-tenths of the copyists are women ? -A. Yes.	,
Q- And the greater part of the extra clerks are women-A. Yes.
Q. Is that because they are content to enter the service _ at a lower rate than $500?-A. 1 think that is the case. Of course, there is a great deal of pressure to get women into the service.
Q. Brom whom?-A. From political friends.
Again :
Q- There is a Treasury Board minute of 1879 about the use of political influence by government employees. Did you ever hear of it?
And the deputy minister, Mr. Butler, one of the most efficient officers we have in the service in Canada answers:
No.

It was passed in 1879 but it is in force. The minister apparently thinks that it should not be enforced because it was passed in 1879, just as al-
Hr. LENNOX
though time was spent by a royal commission in 1892 and valuable information collected, aud it was shown that some evils were capable of being remedied, he still thinks after eleven years in office that they ought not do anything but fold their hands. The chairman says :	[DOT]
I think you had better get a copy of the minute. It lays down the principle that no officer should use political influence. By the mere use of political influence, pro tanto, he renders himself subject to dismissal.
And the deputy answered :
I was inclined to issue such a circular to the men in the outside service.
That is concerning promotion, it is for increase of salary, not appointment.

He was pointing out the fact, as I understand it, that not only was political influence used to get these men into positions, but when they are in positions they use influence to get promotion and defy the head of the department to some extent. For that reason Sir John Macdonald had that minute passed so that every civil servant should know that if he dared to use political influence he was for that reason liable to dismissal forthwith. I hope the minister will take it into his consideration very seriously, because the department referred to is one of the most vulnerable except perhaps the Department of Marine and Fisheries. Political influence is used on that railway in another way.
My hon. friend will note that he did not answer my question. He has not read an item or an extract concerning the Intercolonial Railway or its employees as yet.
Why not?
Because it is a fact.
I am dealing with the evidence of the Depnty Minister of Railways and Canals.
Not concerning the Intercolonial Railway.
Hear, hear.
Why? For political purposes aud for political purposes alone, there is no getting over that fact.
That was not political influence, that originated at the time of confederation, for the purpose of giving to the Canadian manufacturers access to the maritime markets.

We have not finished with this question, but I understood the matter in a different way. I understood we constructed the railway for the purposes of giving communication from the maritime provinces to these provinces and back again, but I did not understand that we ever advertised that we were going to give them anything more than a fair, square deal havins reference to the rights of all the people of Canada.

The only communication between Ontario and the maritime provinces previous to the construction of the Intercolonial Railway, was by way of American seaports and American transportation lines, and in order to divert the traffic through Canadian territory the Intercolonial Railway was constructed and for the same purpose the rates were made inviting.

I have heard that discussed in this House repeatedly and have heard hon. gentlemen from the maritime provinces as familiar with this matter as* the hon. gentleman who has just spoken,' and with just the same facility in expressing themselves as he has, and they have said that there was no discrimination in rates, that they got nothing better than the ordinary rates prevailing on other railways, and no advantage more than they would get from any company railway. We have on the other hand the evidence of the deputy minister that the people in the maritime provinces are getting such rates as no other people get in any portion of the world. That is according to the evidence of the Deputy Minister of Railways and Canals, Mr. Butler.
I wish to give another quotation in that connection.
Q. I mean to say it should be run for the least possible money and made an efficient machine all round?-A. We have got the most efficient railway in Canada, .the best roadbed and the best passenger service you can find in Canada to-day, and we are doing the work for practically 50 per cent less than it costs the other railways, that is to say we are taking out of the customers of the railway not much more than one-half what the other railways are taking.
Q. What do you mean by that?-A. We are not charging the customers of the railway much more than one-half what the other railways are. Our freight rates are much lower, our passenger rates are much the same for the short haul but for the long haul they are lower and we are paying onr men as good wages as the other railways and keeping our standard up to the highest pitch.
I venture to say that evidence will be construed by the majority of thinking people as showing _ that the railway is used to serve local and political purposes rather than the interests of Canada, and we know that to a large extent the deficits on the Intercolonial Railway are attributable to that fact.

Pardon me. That is a very trite question just now, and I know the leader of the opposition will appreciate the question I am going to ask the hon. gentleman-In view of the remarks of my hon. friend is he in favour of increasing the rate for freight and passengers on the Intercolonial ?
I am not going to assist my hon. friend in that regard.
If the rates are wrong the hon. gentleman ought be able to say so.
WTe may have to consider that question at an early date.
Who gets the benefit?

Let me answer one question at a time. We may have to take the matter out of the hands of the Minister of Railways at a very early date and when we do we will deal with it in a way that is fair to all classes interested. Let me refer to another quotation which will deal with the Intercolonial but in another way.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I submit, Mr. Speaker, that the question before us for discussion is the civil service not freight rates on the Intercolonial Railway.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: A discussion of the rates charged on the Intercolonial Railway is not relevant to the question before the House.

I am sorry the right hon. gentleman did not mention the matter sooner because I have finished my reference to it. The witness was speaking about the employment of men on the Intercolonial and the following evidence was given :
Q. Who has the appointment of trackmen?- A. The roadmasters would have the general supervision of the force, say from Riviere du Loup to Obaudaere Junction and then another roadmaster from there 'to Montreal. The road-master holds the foreman of the track responsible for the carrying on of the work. The men are appointed generally on the recommendation of members of parliament in the case of vacancies. That is to say, a man must be a good man; he must be able to make good or he is dropped from the service, but when a vacancy comes the member in whose county the vacancy occurs has the say as to who shall succeed.
I think the patronage system here is more serious than in the aspect in which the Minister of Finance dealt with it this afternoon, because here we are dealing with

the lives of people who .travel upon the Intercolonial railway and we are making appointments not with regard to who are the best or fittest men but upon the recommendation of the member for the county, continuing he is asked :
Q. Do yon not consider that objectionable ?.- A. Well it has worked out fairly satisfactorily.
Q. What about the appointment of engineers and firemen?
That is a more serious matter still because the engineer has the lives of the passengers in his charge and the answer is :
A. In the first instance the fireman or the trackman is liable to be appointed upon the nomination of some political friend, but once he is appointed he has to make good. He joins the brotherhood immediately and works up step by step.
Q. And the majority of the employees, are appointed politically or do they come under the brotherhood?-A. They belong to the brotherhood but they all enter the service in the first instance, I fancy, on the nomination of some member of parliament.
Again Mr. Giroux is examined with regard to the service on the canals and he says :
Q. How did all you people get employment in the beginning?-A. I have been employed two years through Mr. Rivet, my deputy.
Q. Then the member for the district sends your name to the department and you get employment ?-A. Yes, sir.
Q. That applies generally throughout the canals?-A. Yes, sir.
Q. There is no passing examination or anything of that kind?-A. Jfo.
Let me now quote from the evidence of Mr. Fottinger :
Q. Then, in all the shops in the month of August you had 2,467 employees?-A. Yes, all over the line.
Q. Are all these 2,467 men employed in the shops appointed primarily by political nomination?-A. Primarily they are recommended by some supporter of the government. Of course there are exceptions to that sometimes. For instance, mechanics of the machinist olass have been very scarce and we have been compelled to employ, any one who came along in that capacity.
And only when they are compelled do they neglect politics in the matter.
Q. If you found a good class of mechanics coming out as immigrants would the chief superintendent or master mechanic have power to secure their services if he needed them?-A. If he needed them.
Q. Apart from political pressure?-A. Yes.
Q. The appointment of one thousand and odd people in the shops at Moncton gives a good deal of political patronage to the member in that district?-A. I may explain that the Moncton shops have been considered to belong to the whole line and not merely to the county Mr. LENNOX.
in which they are situated although in practice the county gets the majority.
They belong to the whole line for what purpose ? For political pull and nothing else. These men tell all this without a blush :
Q. It has nothing to do with the by-elections?-A. Nothing whatever.
Q. The trackmen are exclusively appointed from the district?	,
They are dealing with the question of men being confined to a particular district and that they dare not be appointed out of their district or else there would be an insurrection amongst the politicians.
Who said that ?

Mr. Fottinger I think. Any how it was sworn to.
Q. It has nothing to do with the by-elections?-A. Nothing whatever.
Q. The .trackmen are exclusively appointed from the districts in which the tracks are laid I suppose; you don't get your trackmen from the county of Rimouski to go into the adjoining county?-A. Well, the track district runs from Ste. Flavie to Camphellton and goes through the counties of Rimouski and Bona-venture and a small part of Restigouche. These trackmen are local people. They are on a certain definite piece of line about six miles long, so that they will naturally fall into the county in which they are employed.
Q. I have heard that trackmen in Rimouski are stopped at the border and replaced by other trackmen in Bonaventure, and that these again are stopped at the border and replaced by trackmen from the next county?-A. I have not heard that in regard to Rimouski, and it would not be the case with respect to trackmen. But there is a class of men that we employ going about on trains cleaning ditches and so on, and it may have occurred in regard to that class of work. It has occurred in Cape Breton.
Q. I have heard the story that at Cape Breton you went through four or five counties, and at the county line one carload of men was dropped and another carload was taken on?-A. That has been the case sometimes, hut they were extra men.
And they were engaged at a time when an election was coming on, for extra political purposes.
That statement is not in the evidence, is it ?
No.
That is a remark of your own ?
That is a remark of my own.
You are drawing on your imagination ?

No, I am not drawing on my imagination. It is borne out by the evidence I have read and the statements of

the Royal Commission appointed by the government ; it is borne out by facts that we have had established before this House from time to time ; and it is true to the knowledge of my hon. friend who has just spoken. Here is another passage :
Q. Now we come to the working expenses. Do you purchase all your stores by lowest tender after advertising?-A. The general storekeeper sends out circulars to the different persons in the trade who are recommended by the members.
Q. -But in the case of big purchases?-A. In regard to ties and lumber we send out posters which are put up at all the stations along the railway, and everybody can tender that wishes to do so. In regard to the large works, they are advertised in the newspapers, and every one who wishes can tender.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: If I am obliged to rule, I shall have to rule.

If you rule, I will stop that branch of the inquiry ; but if you had not ruled, I would have imagined that the question of how the administration is being carried on in regard to the civil service is very pertinent jo the question whether the system proposed in the motion is a better system than the one that has been pursued in the past. However, I have given enough for illustration, and I have referred only to one department. The Department of Marine and Fisheries is full of very much more
startling evidence than that which I have read in reference to the Department of Railways.
Now, the Minister of Finance says that the civil service is open to all. The civil service examinations are open to all, but that is as far as it goes as a matter of actual fact. All can pass the examinations if they think fit, but a very large percentage of the young men and young women of this country who would pass the civil service examinations are deterred by the fact that they know that it would be a mere farce to do so because their chance of getting an appointment is so exceedingly remote. The Minister of Finance knows as well as anybody else that the civil service is not open to all in any other sense than the mere passing of the examinations. To give authority for that statement, let me quote what the Civil Service Commissioners say. At page i5 of their report you will find this statement :
The commissioners also beg to point out that in the list of passed candidates published in the r Canada Gazette J no attention is given to merit.
A matter that was particularly dwelt on by the hon. member for North Toronto, and that merit should be one of the means of securing employment in the civil service, it is essential that a record should be kept of those who have passed the examinations and the order in which they have passed; hut no such record is kept. The one who merely scrapes through is just as likely to get an appointment if he satisfies the political pull, as the candidate who has passed exceedingly high, and the minister knows that as well and even better than I do, if he would only say so. The commissioners go on to say:
The candidates are gazetted, alphabetically. No doubt it has happened that the candidates who have just fluked through the examination by means of greater political influence have recedvd appointments over the heads of more worthy and better qualified candidates.
In the matter of promotions the same patronage fear is apparent. Your commissioners found in their rounds that a collector of customs, a city postmaster, a post office inspector and others were appointed politically. The recent appointment of a postmaster at Kingston was on the recommendation of the patronage committee; the last appointment to the postmastership at Montreal, the most important in the Dominion, was given to an aged member of parliament, 67 years old.
I will not say more upon this question now.
Hear, hear.

If it were not effective I do not think the bon. gentleman would be anxious for me to sit down; but as it is not suiting their purpose and is not advancing their interests, they are anxious that I should give it up. Well, I am not going to

try my case in their court. I am going to a higher and more responsible tribunal. When I find that bon. gentlemen opposite are restless, it rather inspires me with the belief that I am doing good service to the country by proceeding a little further.
Will you stop if we cry 'go on ' ?

I will stop when I think I have fully discharged my duty. I want to refer to a few extracts from the report of the royal commissioners. Speaking of the Militia Department, they say :
There are officers enough in the department, both inside and outside, to do all the work efficiently, if they were properly trained and 'organized; hut there is no efficient organization. The only attempt at it is the appointment of men whose titles would seem to indicate what their duties are; but those duties have never been specifically defined. There is no record of anything of the bind, and there are no written or printed rules and regulations known in the service, which your commissioners think is lamentable.
It is practically impossible to fix responsibility on anybody. The deputy is supposed to shoulder responsibility for everything ias his signature shows; but that means that he speaks for ' the department,' and ' the department,' like the King, can do no wrong. There seems to be a huge redundancy of work which proceeds in a lumbering, haphazard way, giving rise to constant blundering and confusion. There is no sign visible of a single directing head, or an intelligent purpose, unless it be that of spending as much money as possible. Zeal for economy and good management, or pride in the work, is not visible. Perfunctory and mechanical discharge of duties is the rule, with apparently no perception of any need for improvement.
Then the commissioners go on to deal with the question of bookkeeping by the Faulkner Company. They point out:
After months of work by the highly paid experts the result has been at least greatly improved books as far as mechanical reform is concerned, but probably little else; and this .achievement has been accomplished at an almost fabulous expense.
There is not only a lack of efficient organization and method in the department. There would also seem to be a lack of conscience. In connection with the enormous expenditures which are deemed necessary, the word ' discount ' never appears. It is tacitly assumed that there is no such thing; but the whole commercial world knows otherwise. If no one gets any benefit from trade with the government except the trader, then it must be clear that in these great purchases made for the government, without discount, its officers must be assisting the trader to get better prices from the government than he can get anywhere else; for, everywhere else he has to I give discount. In other words, some of the government's officers aire serving two masters, and apparently succeeding with both-scripture notwithstanding.
It is certain that under such a state of

things it must he impossible to develop high character in the service, or rather to prevent the deterioration of what character there is.
As some evidence that the heads of the department have been quite aware of it, we find on one of the files a memorandum by one of the" officers dated May 31, 1905, regarding expenditures in connection with lighthouses. ' I *am of opinion that in the Quebec agency alone a saving of at least $25,000 per annum can be made by compelling the agent to obtain authority for his expenditures over ordinary supplies and maintenance. If this is not carried out, the department can look for an overdraft for the next fiscal year of from $50,000 to $100,000.'
The cure suggested is too ludicrous to be taken seriously, but, as evidence of the condition of things,, and the department's knowledge of it, this memorandum is significant. It was marked approved and initialled by the minister at that time.
Coming to the question of the lighthouse board-this scheme which was adopted for purposes which I do not think the government would like very fully to explain-the commissioners say :
Between June, 1905, and June, 1907, this board approved of and passed applications for new and improved aids to navigation amounting to $1,691,813. With the voting away of this vast amount of money the responsible minister had nothing to do. He was simply asked to initial the minutes of the different meetings of this most powerful but irresponsible board. The effect of this state of things is disastrous. It means practically the removing of all responsibility from those to whom extensive powers of administration and expenditure are granted.
When one realizes the enormous pressure being constantly brought to hear on the government of the day in favour of grants and bounties of all kinds, from one end of the country to the other, it would surely seem to be a most unwise thing to create a board with extensive powers, which can be and are used in sympathy with this universal outside pressure, and without being accountable to anybody.
The two outside members of this board simply represent the shipping interest, which is their own. They cannot serve the country and themselves equally well in the same matter. The other members of the hoard are government officials, who, whatever their standing may be, personally or officially, are not independent of political influence or departmental pressure. They are in no proper sense qualified to fill such a position of trust as a seat on this lighthouse board should mean-where the most absolute sense of justice, with complete independence, is called for; with a keen desire to administer the people's money with the utmost economy and good judgment, and with all prsonal considerations sunk.
There can be very little question that the lighthouse board has been the means of greatly increasing the expenditure of the department, and that much of the increase has been wasted.
It is pretty clearly urged, so that I need not stop to emphasize it, that that board

is an utterly irresponsible body, utterly unconstitutional and one which never should have been created. And when the opportunity now presents itself, we should avail ourselves of it to have a better system than we now have. Again :
Your commissioners have to confess that the general conclusions which they have formed regarding the administration of the department are most unfavourable. It seems to have few redeeming features; although there are some, one of which is the presence in the department of some good men, chiefly, but not wholly, in the lower ranks. . . Organization, discipline, zeal for the public service, and regard for economy are all conspicuous by their absence.
A word or two about the Department of Militia may not be out of place. The commissioners say :
The expenditure in this department is going up by leaps and bounds. In 1903-4 the total expenditure, both in capital and consolidated fund, was in the neighbourhood of three and a half million dollars. In the estimates lately submitted to parliament for the fiscal year ending March 31, 1909, appropriations are asked for aggregating $6,500,000. That is to say, in four years and three-quarters the expenditures will have increased, if the supply asked for is granted, to the extent of $3,000,000.
About the Militia Council also they have something to say :
In addition to the council an officer has been appointed, called the inspector general, at a salary of $6,000 per -annum. In Great Britain the appointment of inspector general was made for reasons which do not exist in Canada; -but as the inspector general in Canada has only to report, your commissioners are very doubtful, however valuable the reports may be, that the retention of an officer at such a large salary is beneficial and altogether in the public interests. From past experience, it would seem as if this office were being made a stepping stone to the retirement of high military officers in Canada on large allowances.
Then summing up they say :
In conclusion your commissioners have to point out that the expenditure has grown in a little over four years from -three and a half millions to six and a half millions; that the permanent and headquarters staff have increased to the number of about 220; that in addition to the general system of high pay the favoured men of the militia service in Canada draw pensions ont only for themselves but for their wives and ohildren; that the staff is sufficient for a corps of one hundred thousand men according to the evidence submitted; that the desertions have been one in three; thht the number of militia trained in the annual camps is about 40,000 men; that according to the evidence of Major General Lake the men attached to the rural battalions have no drill except at the annual camps, and it is arguable whether the city corps are as efficient as they were so-me years ago; that while only 40,000 men came out for drill of ages from 18 to 50, 293
yet compared with the population of over a million men in Canada between the ages of 20 and 40, the proportion seems small. Whether with all the large expenditure of public moneys the result as detailed shows efficiency, your commissioners leave to the consideration of Your Excellency.
I had intended to read the account submitted through the commissioners of the difference in expenditure in the Militia Department now and in 1904, but I will not now take the time necessary for that purpose. I think the instances given prove with abundant clearness that the time has come when we should have a thorough revision of our civil service along the lines marked out by the resolution of my hon. friend from North Toronto (Mr. Foster). And, whatever the right hon. Prime Minister may say as to this being an inopportune time, I am sure the country believes that the time is most opportune for bringing in a measure along these lines. We shall await with interest the bringing in of the government measure to see if it carries out the main recommendations of the Civil Service Commission which the right hon. gentleman appointed and whether it is framed along lines which will leave these appointments and promotions free from political influences. In the meantime I shall have great pleasure in supporting the amendment.

Is it the intention, of the government to keep us longer here to-night 1
I would like to pass one or two items.

We came here at 3 o'clock this afternoon, and it is now after 12. We have debated a very important resolution this afternoon. We are, we will suppose, Christians and men, and I do not think we have any right, either on one side or the other, to strain our endurance to an unnecessary point. It does seem to me that if we are called upon to sit much later than 12 o'clock at night it is straining to a point of endurance which is unreasonable, at this time of the year and in this kind of weather. The plea is made that it is necessary to get through business. So it is; but there is other business than the estimates that are before the House, and this House cannot prorogue until the other business as well as the estimates are carried through. We might as well be frank with each other, and say that there are some points of legislation about which there is a difference, that difference has existed for some time, and although it has existed for some time, we seem to be no nearer getting a decision from the government as to whether they propose to press that legislation or not. I think the government ought to treat us fairly and frankly, and they will find the opposition anxious with them in putting through the other necessary business of the session.

I have no desire to keep the House late, but 1 will tell you how the thing stands. I want to get $2,074,500. It is all in one item, it generally passes like that. We are only asking for what is necessary. To-day we should have drawn our cheques to pay our outside officers. I suppose there are 2,000 men who, if you do not give them this money, will have to go without their pay. The hon. gentleman speaks about it being un-Christian to sit late. Would it not be more un-Christian to put us in the position of being unable to pay men who, we have been told to-night, have been faithful men and who have well earned their wages ? At any rate, so far as I am concerned, and I think I have my colleagues and the Prime Minister with me, I will make an effort to get the money, so that these men who are under my charge cannot at any rate lay the blame upon me if they go without the wages which they have fairly earned. I will give what explanations members may desire. I suppose there are a hundred men in this city alone who will have to go without the pay they have earned if I do not get this money, and others are scattered from the Atlantic to the Pacific; too many of them, as hon. gentlemen opposite know, do not get salaries that enable them to do without their money when it is due. Therefore

I desire to stay long enough at any rate to let those gentlemen know that the head of the department is not to blame if they do not get their money.

There is another way in which the situation can be stated. I do not propose to be put in the wrong by the specious reasoning of the (Minister of Customs. It is perfectly right that these men who do the work should have their pay and these men would have had their pay many days before this if the government had not obtruded between them and their pay obnoxious legislation, obnoxious to a large portion of this House and the country. The government have it within their power in a very short time to allow these men to get their pay by withdrawing, or by putting aside, a portion of the legislation which is not necessary to the well being of this country, either to the Department of Customs or to any other department of the service. It is a party interest purely and simply which is involved in that legislation, and it is obtruded, not in the interest of the service of the country but of the party.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There is a large batch of legislation proposed, which stands on the Order Paper, but because the hon. gentleman differs from us as respects some portion of that legislation, therefore the customs officers shall not get their money.
