Last year we went into a general increase and I have a list of all to whom increases wtere given, but it is very long and I suppose I need not read it. There will be some deserving cases this year and we would like to have tine money if it is decided we should grant them. There are continual demands on the Customs Department for new ports and officers are required at these ports. This is not all for the collection of revenue because we have had during the past year 15 or 20 men who do nothing in the way of collecting revenue but who are safeguarding the revenue. We have adopted a more stringent system of inspection and put on an additional staff at several points near the frontier.,, The only question to be considered is: Is $80,000 too much to grant for deserving additions to salaries and for providing for the extra work that will come upon the department.

What is the reason of the provision:
Salaries and contingent expenses of the several -ports including pay for overtime of officers, notwithstanding anything in the Civil Service Act.

Office hours are from 8 to 6 and we have officers who meet trains coming in at night and have to be paid for their overtime. In old tirrues the transportation companies paid this charge, but some years ago parliament decided to pay it out of the public funds.

This is a matter which is very strongly criticised in the civil service neport and that criticism I entirely concur in. If your Civil Service Act at

present does not permit you to carry on the business of the country as it should be [DOT]carried on why not amend it ? It is not advisable to have a provision in item aftier item declaring that it is in contravention of the Civil Service Act.
This has been going on for years and years.
And unless it is stopped it will go on for ever.
It has bieen going on more than ever for the last ten years.
Oh, no.

Would the Minister of Customs explain what is meant by this statement in the report of the Civil Service Commission:
The chief positions in the outside service of this department are political appointments. Every collector of customs has been appointed from the ranks of the party in power at the moment.
When vacancies occur you have to fill them. My desire always is to fill them with competent men, men of character and men of ability. That I try my best to do.
What examinations?
Collectors of customs have not to pass the civil service examination.
The position of the Minister of Customs is that there is no use in Conservatives passing the examination because they would not get the appointment.
I did not say that.
Well, the commissioners say as much.

I do not know what the commissioners may say. I have the recommendations, but I do not know the parties personally, and I have to avail myself of the knowledge of those who do know them to assure myself that they are competent; and if a man is competent for the position, the fact that he is a Liberal is not a barrier to his appointment.
Has there been a Conservative appointed since my hon. frieDd has been Minister of Customs ?
I think the officers have been largely drawn from the Liberal party.

I notice that the commissioners distinctly state that almost all the appraisers in the outside service of this department, have been appointed without undergoing the civil service examination ; and yet the minister gave us to Mr. R. L. BORDEN.
understand that they have undergone this examination.
I did not say that.
Does the hon. minister then not think it would be wise for them to undergo some examination and be properly fitted to fill these positions ?
Yes, I think it would.
The report distinctly says they do not.

Well, I do not agree with ail that the report says. An appraiser does not undergo the civil service examination, but he has-to undergo, under the authority of the Civil Service Act, a practical examination in the duties of his office. I do not care how literary a character a man may be, if he has not handled any dry goods, groceries, crockery, boots and shoes and other articles of merchandise, his knowledge, valuable as it would be in certain spheres, is not sufiicient for an appraiser of goods. We have men of education and intelligence and also with a practical knowledge which enables them to know what line of goods come under a certain rate of duty, what item applies to them, and the character and value of the goods. That kind of an examination they undergo.
I cannot help reading a few more lines of this report and asking the Minister of Customs what he intends to do regarding these statements made by the Commission.

Write him a letter.
Mi'. ARMSTRONG. I [DOT] am afraid the minister would not read it. I wish to impress this upon him :
The only suggestion the commissioners can make in regard to the outside service is to have the service absolutely divorced from political influence and have all the appointments put on a basis of merit.
These are strong assertions. I do not see how the Minister of Customs can get over them. He frankly admits that he only appoints Liberals.
They were mostly all Conservatives.

My hon. friend would almost as lief appoint a Doukhobor on the railway as a Conservative, and perhaps rather. I think we are justified in asking the minister whether he intends to carry out the policy, in spite of the commissioners' report, that no men shall be appointed in the Customs Department, unless they are political partisans of his, and the commissioners distinctly state that the men are not fitted for the positions they are filling.

As I said before, I do not hold myself bound by all that the commissioners have said. They formed their opinions, and I think they did right to express them ; but I have my opinions . too, and I think perhaps I know as much about the service, having been connected with it for ten years, as a gentleman who called up one or two of my officers and examined them. If my hon. friend reads that report, I think he will find that the testimony given to the commissioners was that on the whole the customs staff was a valuable body of men discharging their duties well.
Is the payment for overtime in addition to the ordinary pay of these officials, or is it deducted from their salaries ?

It supplements their regular statutory salary. Up to last year the rate was 25 cents an hour, but last year parliament gave me permission to raise it to 30 cents an hour. Where we require men to work overtime on Sundays, we pay them, and the amount is recouped to us by the transportation companies. Otherwise we pay them the extra amount.
Are many men affected by this regulation ?
Yes, a large number- in Montreal, in Halifax and in St. John.

These men must work many hours overtime, judging by the amounts they redeive. A great many have advanced from $200 to $300. There is overtime like that to the extent of over $18,000. I cannot understand what overtime they do except on Sundays. Are the temporary employees, those who work on the wharfs in the summer-about $11,000 ? When are they employed and how long ?
There is overtime at the stations in winter but the most is in the summer.

I do not understand why a man under salary, when there is work to do, should not come back and do it. In commercial offices, if there is need for the clerks to go back after eight o'clock, they do so and are not paid overtime. This sort of expenditure used to be very much criticised by my hon. friend when in opposition but we have more of it now than ever.
What is the total amount which goes for overtime ?
How is that distributed?
It is distributed at Montreal, Quebec and the various other ports according as the work is done
How does the minister arrive at that $90,000 ?

The accountant makes up his estimates and he knows what was paid last year. He estimates whether the amount is likely to be increased. He cannot tell the exact amount. We may have occasion to appoint an extra officer during the year, which appointment could not be foreseen, and that might reduce a little the overtime at that particular port, but the estimate is fairly accurate.
What number of hours do these men work in their regular service?
Ten hours per day.
Who selects the men to do the overtime ?

The collectors at the different ports. Mr. White, collector at Montreal, apportions the men there. There is great desire among the men, who have small salaries, to share in the overtime, and Mr. White endeavours to divide it as fairly as he can. We have to trust to our collectors.

What supervision has the department over this matter of overtime ? Mr. White may be a very trustworthy collector but all collectors may not be the same. Here you have $90,000 voted by parliament, and that can be practically expended exactly as the collectors wish. In the first place is the overtime work necessary ? What check has the minisfer ? If necessary, what is the method on which the men are assigned to the work ? How does the minister satisfy himself that this $90,000 has to be expended ? If due diligence were used and if proper work were done within the hours, it would not be necessary.
The collector has to certify to the extra time.
But is the extra time necessary ? Is there any system of inspection or check ?
Yes.
What is it ?

We have a tide surveyor on the wharf at all hours of the night, and we have the surveyor of the port who will be up at night at all hours very often, and these have to certify, before the money is paid, that the work has been done. And the men get two hours and not more, as a rule, because we think that if a man works twelve hours that is enough. So, we do not allow him to work more than two hours overtime.

As I understand the collectors make a demand for a certain amount for their ports, which amount is placed in their hands. They have to choose the persons who should do the overtime. But that is limited by the two hours maximum. I suppose it is possible that favour-

itism may be shown. I am not saying that it is shown, but such a thing is possible. But what check has the minister to prove that the men have actually performed two hours overtime and have done their work faithfully ?
The only check we can possibly have-the certificates of the men who employ them.
That is the collector, but he is not there at all hours.
He has his subordinate officers.
But who certifies ?
The tide surveyor on the wharf, or the landing waiter at the railway.
What work do the overtime men do ?

For instance, wait at the station until a train comes in to examine the baggage of people who want to go through that night instead of putting the baggage in bond. This is a convenience to the railways, so much so that in days gone by they paid for it themselves. Ships coming in also want facilities for quick unloading. And goods have to be watched at night. Of course, there are night watchmen, and I suppose that the man who is up at night is not up in the day time. If the hon. gentleman (Mr. Poster) will think it over, he will see that it is difficult to suggest any other plan than the one we have. We cannot send a man from here to look after it. If we have officers upon whom we cannot rely, we might be lost, but we have confidence in them. Nothing of that kind could go wrong in the port without our hearirig it.
Suppose that John Jones and John Smith are detailed for overtime work at a railway station. Their regular hours end at what time ?
Six o'clock.
If a train is due at eleven o'clock, are these men detailed to go at that time and do two hours' work up to one o'clock ? Or do you arrange that every train and ship should come in at six o'clock.
No.
Then how is it arranged ? Is a man detailed to go down at eleven o'clock and put in his two hours' work ?
Yes, if he did not start the two hours before.

That is pretty hard on the service, is it not ? A man must be roused from his rest at eleven o'clock to go down Mr. FOSTER.
to do two hours' work. Or it may be that the train does not come in until one o'clock.
It is hard on them.
But is it not hard on the service 3 When a man is engaged in extra work in this way, you can hardly expect him to be fresh for his regular ten hours' work next day. How does it work out in practice ?

It works out satisfactorily. The only other way would be to engage enough men to have a day staff and a night staff. Many of these men, if they had not overtime, would want their salaries increased, because they could not get on with the wages they have. So, not only would you have to pay the salaries of the larger staff, but you would have to pay these men more as well. Therefore, this is the most economical method. These men are not engaged in hard physical labour. They have to wait for an hour or two, perhaps, in order to do a half hour's work.
If the man waits there and is not called upon to do any work, does he get his time just the same ?

He does the work by being there. This to help trade and commerce. That it is a help is shown by the fact that the railways were willing to pay for it, but, instead of letting them pay, we pay it ourselves.
Suppose a man goes down at eight o'clock and the train does not come in until ten, and after it comes in he does two hours' work. Is he paid for four hours?
No. He would be relieved by another man or the goods would go into bond.
But if he were not relieved he would get his pay?
Yes, but the goods would probably go into bond after 12 o'clock at night.
Prom the minister's explanation it seems to be a very haphazard arrangement.	,
I do not see how it is more so than any other part of the system by which our $10,000,000 or $15,000,000 is collected.

So far as attending the trains is concerned, I should think you might embrace that in the daily duty of some officer, letting him begin his work in the day at a later hour. Of course, I can understand how he should have overtime if the train is late. But when you expect a train every day in the year at a stated hour, it is a matter almost of necessity to have some one there in order to transact

the business of the customs. Now, why should we call that overtime?
We are working overtime now. They put in their ten hours and if they put in two hours more we pay them for it.

Suppose a train comes in at 8 o'clock at night or 6 o'clock in the morning, and you know it is expected at that hour every day in the year, why is it necessary to deal with it as something unusual when you know that in the ordinary course it will come in at those hours ?
The hon. gentleman would not advocate an officer having two hours of his time taken up without paying him?
I did not suggest anything of the kind.

A train arrives at 8 o'clock, we will suppose, in the morning at Winnipeg or Montreal. The cartage company start working at 7 o'clock in the morning; they want to get their goods, and we must have certain officers there. It is a piece of economy to pay certain officers overtime instead of having a regular staff for the purpose.

If you require the service of a man at 6 o"'clock in the morning let him leave at a corresponding earlier hour in the afternoon, or if there is another train at 8 o'clock or 10 o'clock in the evening, let the man who has to deal with that begin his work at a later hour in the day.
that the minister asks us to vote for salaries.
And about how much for contingent expenses?
About $150,000. As a matter of fact, the expenditure for nine months for salaries to the 31st of October amounted to $940,895.
What was expended last year for salaries ?
Last year the expenditure was $1,601,000 for those three items.
That is exactly the demerit of this vote. It is a concealed ^ote, and I would like to have it definitely on ' Hansard ' so that we may have something on which to bring the minister up.
For the nine months the salaries were $869,885.50 ; overtime, $60,636.35 ; and contingencies, $78,938.70.
What is the anticipated increase in overtime ?

I cannot state definitely what portion of the $80,000 will be used but approximately it is estimated that we will require $50,000 for increased salaries and $30,000 for additional officers and increased expenditure on contingencies.
How do you divide that ?
We do not divide them, we cannot tell that until it is expended.
What the hon. gentleman suggests can be done, but it can only be done by adding to the staff.
As the minister has shown us where $90,000 of this vote is to be found, what is the gross amount that is estimated for salaries?
It would be the balance of that vote.

No, there are other items. This brings out again the concealed nature of these votes and the impossibility of having any parliamentary control over them. You have here $1,750,000, and for anything that is contained in the direction of this vote you can spend a million of that on overtime, or half a million of it on contingent expenses, and you can call anything you like a contingent expense. Now, that kind of vote is the blindest, and that 'is the least responsible way of making up estimates. It gives the minister power that he ought not to have, because it puts the whole amount of money into his hands and he can appropriate just as much as he pleases to each of the three divisions. I would like to know what is the amount
The Minister should have his estimate.
I do not think it is at all necessary. I am asking for the vote and it will be paid as it has been in the past.
The lack of definite estimate in these votes does not lead to economy of expenditure or to the clearness the House wants before giving money to the minister.

If I should give a definite estimate, say $10,000, it may not be correct. New lines of steamers may run to this country or new lines of railway enter and in that way the information given now might be misleading.

You have estimated for over time, salaries, and contingencies on the general run of your business in the past. All we want is that the minister should cut up his $80,000 into what would be required for each of these three divisions.
That is done in I the estimates of other departments.

In the old times it used to be done for each province but if you ran short of your estimate for one province and had more than sufficient for another province you would not be allowed to take the overplus and a supplementary estimate had to be brought down for the province with respect to which there was a deficiency. We are one Dominion and it is the same service, and it is a far better plan to take the vote for the whole Dominion.

I do not advocate any division by provinces. Why should not this huge item of nearly $3,000,000 be divided so that we might see how much goes for each service ? I am opposed to supplementary estimates and for my part I would be prepared to give the minister a liberal allowance so that he would not be obliged at the end of the year to resort to a supplementary estimate.

The Minister of Customs must not go away with the idea that I want the old division by provinces. We are one Dominion and the vote is for the service of the Dominion, but there is no reason why it should not be divided so that we may see what goes for each service. Under the English system the estimates are submitted to the House with great minuteness of detail and explanations are even given in the estimates, which is much better than trying to get it by question and answer from an unwilling minister as appears to be at present the case. We have got so far that we are told that there is $50,000 for increases in salaries ; is that a guess of the minister ?
It is an estimate.
It is not founded on making up your mind as to who ought have increases of salary.
That has not been considered yet. I have applications for, increases from various officers and I told them I had not money to pay their salaries to say nothing of giving them increases.

Before the minister asks $50,000 to increase the salaries of officers should he not lay before the House the grounds upon which he considers these officers are entitled to increases ? Is parliament or is the minister to be the judge of that ? If increases are asked for under the civil government appropriation we are told what officers are to get increases.
The Act provides for that.
The proper time to consider what officers you should increase is before you ask parliament for a vote for

h. BORDEN.
that purpose. It must be assumed that parliament will ask what officers are going to get increases of salaries and the minister should have that information. Will the minister tell us what collectors are to get increases ?
I do not know.
If the minister does not know he had better not ask for this appropriation.
If you don't give it to me all right.

It is all very well for the minister to say that, but we should have the information before we vote the money. The time for the minister to make up his mind as to what officers shall get an increase in salary is before he asks parliament for the money. The hon. minister had better take the trouble of getting the information for the committee before he asks it to vote. Why does he want this $50,000 ? Whose salaries is he going to increase ? He does not know, but he wants to be the beneficent father and get the lump sum from parliament without giving the information as to wliat he wants it for, and then scatter it around as he pleases. It is parliament that should decide whether a man should have an increase or not.
How do you know whether a man should have an increase or not ?

The government might as well come down at once and in a single line ask for $100,000,000 for the expenses of the government; that is the reductio ad absurdum of the hon. gentleman's position, the minister knows that that is not the proper way to put estimates before a committee. So I want to ask the minister again what he proposes to spend in extra overtime, what he proposes to expend in extra contingent expenses and what salaries he proposes to increase for this $25 increase with this $50,000, and what reasons he has giving any increases.

There was $150,000 odd voted last year for increases of salaries, and that was given without a word. The proper criticism would be, what did you do with the money voted last year ? I have the list of payments here. The hon. gentleman asks me how much I propose to spend in overtime next year. I am asking for $10,000 more, but I do not propose to spend a cent of it if I can help it; but I may be compelled under our rule of paying thirty cents an hour to spend the whole of it, or perhaps only $6,000 or perhaps only $5,000.

The minister knows that he has to tell this committee what money he wants and the purpose for which he

wants it. After having been entrusted last year with money on these conditions, it is his duty to answer our questions as to what he did with the moneys entrusted to him last year, and then we will compare the results with his promises. But before he gets this vote, I want him to tell us what he proposes to do with the increase we are giving him this year. If he is going to increase salaries, let us know whose salaries he intends to increase.
Ask that next year.

I want it this year, before he has expended the money. The minister is clearly up against it. Before he gets this vote, he has to tell this committee what he proposes to do with this money. Is the minister ready to tell us that?
I have told you what I have to say.
But you have not told us what we want to know. The minister has no more information?
No.
I will let that simmer for a while. What are the different grades of officers and how much money is devoted to the salaries of each grade ?
You will find the officers in the Civil Service List.
What are your principal officers?

The principal officer in Montreal is Robert White. Under the Civil Service Act we have collectors, inspectors, surveyors, assistant surveyors, tide surveyors, chief landing waiters. Then there are technical officers. Then there are clerks in the customs office.
You have collectors first ?
Yes.
What amount of this money goes to pay the collectors ?
The amount they are paid now.
How much is that ?
At the ports of Toronto, Montreal and I think Winnipeg they are paid $4,000 ; at Quebec and Halifax I think $3,200.

Is the minister going to take into consideration the services of the collector of customs at Charlottetown in a matter respecting the infringement of the Inland Revenue Act ? The charge was laid before him that a certain firm of tobacco manufacturers in Charlottetown had committed during 1907 infringements of the law with respect to the placing of stamps on the tobacco
manufactured by them. The matter was represented to the officers of the Inland Revenue Department but they did not see fit to discharge their duty. Probably they did not know what it was or they may have believed that no infringement had taken place. The complainants consequently were compelled to go to to the collector of customs at Charlottetown, Mr. W. B. Robinson, a very worthy gentleman and a good officer. Mr. Robinson informed the commissioner of customs of the complaint made. Previous to Mr. Robinson's information to the department, some communications took place between the officers of the Inland Revenue Department at Charlottetown and the deputy head in Ottawa. At the request of the parties who were aggrieved, I moved for the papers and an order was voted on March 16, in consequence of which the papers were laid on the table. The case may be one the minister may not have heard of, although I know it was before his deputy commissioner and he referred it to the Inland Revenue Department. It is now I consider, my duty to lay it before the Minister of Customs and the Minister of Inland Revenue in order that they may see that justice is done the parties aggrieved and the public. The first communication is as follows :
Inland Revenue Division No. 1, Charlottetown,
Prince Edward Island,
August 5, 1907.
W. J. Gerald, Esq.,
Deputy Minister of Inland Revenue, Ottawa.
Sir,-I have the honour to state that rumours of tobacco being sold ' out of packages ' have reached this office. Kings county seems to be the habitat. I have requested Inspector Burke to come over sooner than usual, although he is due some time this mouth when we might make some arrangements to make seizures. In the meantime I have sent officer Moore to one or two places to investigate and have also instructed him on his collecting tours to visit shops where tobacco is sold and seize in every case illicitly exposed tobacco. I have made requisition to-day for forms.
Question-Is it necessary to remove tobacco seized. I mean to take possession.
I am your obedient servant,
(Sgd.) SAMUEL C. NASH, Collector Inland Revenue.
This Is the answer :
Ottawa, August 8, 1907.
S. C. Nash, Esq.,
Collector of Inland Revenue, Charlottetown, Prince Edward Island.
Sir,-I am in receipt of your communication of the 5th instant respecting the rumoured sale of unstamped tobacco within your division and requesting to be advised as to the necessity for taking possession of such tobacco in case of seizure.
In reply thereto I beg to state that if tobacco is so seized it becomes the property of the Crown and if the facts warrant its seizure

they certainly necessitate taking possession of the goods .seized.
In connection of the matter of seizure of tobacco, out of stamped packages, great care should be used by our officials to endeavour to ascertain if it is a case of fraud or of simple ignorance of the law. While it is true thiat the latter is no justification for the wrong-doing it is a factor that should have some weight with our officials. .
In any case whether tobacco is so found or not our officer should explain to dealers visited the provisions of the law respecting the sale of tobacco and, if these dealers have not been supplied with circular G.-155, a copy thereof should he delivered to each person visited and should be mailed to persons who are not so personally called upon.
I remain, sir,
Yonr obedient servant,
Deputy Minister.
The next communication came from the Hickey & Nicholson Tobacco Company, Charlottetown. It seems that although these reports were made to the officers of the Inland Revenue Department, no notice was taken of them with the exception of the letter I have just read. The parties aggrieved are the Hickey & Nicholson Tobacco Company, Limited, who were doing business In Charlottetown as manufacturers of tobacco. They were informed by their selling agent that tobacco was being sold throughout Prince Edward Island with only one-half stamp upon the packages.
Surely this discussion is not in order in connection with the salaries of customs officers.
Absolutely in order.

These tobaccos were sold at lower prices than the ordinary manufacturer could sell them. The Hickey & Nicholson .Manufacturing Company believed a fraud was committed, not only upon the public, but upon the government of Canada, and by reason of the fact that the company could not obtain the services of the Inland Revenue officials In order to ferret out the guilty parties they went to the collector of customs in Charlottetown.
But Mr. Nicholson thought he would not get justice at their hands and wrote this letter to Mr. Robertson.
Charlottetown, P.E.I.,
August 9, 1907.
W. B. Robertson, Esq.,
'Collector of Customs.
Sir,-Our Mr. Harnett has drawn my attention to gross violations of the Excise and Customs Act and I have reported the same to other officers some time ago hut up to the present no action has been taken or likely to. I therefore report same to you now and demand that you take immediate action and Mr. A. A. McLEAN.
our Mr. Harnett will accompany you to the identical goods.
Yours respectfully,
(Sgd.) HICKEY & NICHOLSON,
Tobacco Company, Ltd. '

Mr. Robertson, in pursuance of the information which he had received, went to Lower Montague and discovered Irregularities with respect to some tobacco sold by the firm of T. B. & D. J. Riley, and that fraud had been committed against the people and government of this country. He reported it to the Commissioner of Customs.

1 renew the point of order that I have already raised. All this has nothing to do with the customs and therefore is irrelevant. My hon friend (Mr. A. A. McLean) is reading from a return which he moved for with respect to certain violations of the excise law in Prince Edward Island. It has no connection with the customs, except that complaint was made to the collector of customs at Charlottetown.
Then there was a connection between the Inland Revenue and the Customs officer.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: Complaint was made to the customs officer-but he had nothing to do with it.
Y<es, he had.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: He wrote two letters. But that has no connection, with the item under discussion. It has to do with the Inland Revenue Department. And if, when my items are under discussion, the hon. gentleman desires explanations and cares to read the entire return in order to get it on ' Hansard ' there will be no objection. In this case, action was taken and a fine was imposed.
No fine was imposed.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: I submit that this has nothing to do with the Item under discussion.

Speaking on the point
of order-
A point of order is not debatable in committee.

I regret to see these evidences of jealousy between the Minister of Inland Revenue and the Minister of Customs. The' Minister of Inland Revenue seems jealous of the fact that the officer of his department had nothing to do with it, but it was strange that he should manifest that feeling so openly in the House. This, however, is merely preliminary, and I believe that preliminary remarks have been held by the chairman to be in order. As

to the point of order, I think that the Min-^ Inland Revenue has answered himself, for he stated that action was taken by an official of the Customs department.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext:
I did not admit anything of the kind.
Mr. FOWLER, But the officer did act. Does the minister pretend to contradict a statement made in a tteport by this official9 Surely he will not have-to use an expression of one of these hon. gentlemen this afternoon-the audacity to quiestion the statement of the Mr. Robertson, the collector of customs, who is a reputable man, a man of irreproachable character.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext:
My point is that it is not relevant.
Mr. FOWLER, But why not. The collector of customs was appealed to and acted.
A point of order cannot be discussed in committee.

It must be discussed. How otherwise is the chairman going to know how to rule?
I am within my rights in discussing this matter. I think that the minister .should consider the smallness of his salary, and increase it. Here is the answer which Mr. Robertson returned after he 'had made his investigation :
Department of Customs, port of Charlottetown, Prince Edward Island.
August 10, 1907.
Sir,-I beg to report that acting on the inclosed letter from the Hickey & Nicholson Company, Limited, I drove to Lower Montague, and called on the firm of W. A. Poole & Company, and while they hare no tobacco on hand at the present moment irregularly stamped, I gleaned enough evidence from Mr. George Poole, a member of the firm, to satisfy me that things are not straight so far as the stamping of the tobacco sent out by the firm of T. B. & D. J. Riley, of this city, are concerned, and I am confident that the circumstances are such as would justify a searching investigation and trust that all may meet with your honourable approval.
I have the honour to be, sir,
Your obedient servant,
(Sgd.) W. B. ROBERTSON, John MoDougald, Esq.,
'Commissioner of Customs, Ottawa, Ontario.
The salary of this same officer is included in this itiem.

Yes. Aud surely we have a right to discuss his salary. I appeal to the Postmaster General (Mr Lemieux) ou this point. I would not appeal to either the Minister of Customs (Mr. Paterson) or the Minister of Inland Revenue (Mr. Templeman) because they are interested and could hardly be expected to give a fair opinion. But I would like the Postmaster General to say whether, when the salary of this officer is under discussion, we have not the right to discuss what this officer did?

There are two reasons why I asked for this to be discussed and why I consider I have the right to disr cuss it. The first reason is that Mr. Robertson, collector of customs, has done a great public service in exposing fraud in tike Inland Revenue. But you won't let me have the money to pay the men even their regular wages.

speechtext: We did ; we got money on account.

speechtext: We ask you now.

speechtext: He is well represented.
I really think we must go on with the discussion of this important matter until we finish it or reach some conclusion. I come to the case of Mr Sanders, of Athelstane. That is not a seaport ?
No, but it is a manifesting port where an American railway comes in.
I hope the minister will not revise his argument. He said that this was confined to seaports.
No.
I understood the minister to say, definitely, positively, absolutely and for the last time that only at the seaports did men work for more than two hours extra.
No, no, tut, tut!
My hon. friend from Yale-Cariboo (Duncan Ross) may have been sleeping-
Tlnere are dozens of international ports where railways cross every Sunday and the customs officers have to work overtime. Everybody except the hon. member (Mr. Lennox) knows that.
But if there were one hundred thousand such points that would not affect the question. The minister said that this was confined to the seaports.
I said that at the seaports they were allowed to get five hours In the summer time.

I am ready to take the minister's explanation, if he will make it clear. I asked the minister as to this two hours overtime running into five hours. And he mentioned that that was confined to the seaports.
I understand that.

Well, the member for Yale-Cariboo being answered, I will proceed with the case of Mr. Sanders, of Athel-stane. This gentleman has a salary of $525 and overtime of $360. There is no possibility at two hours a day, even if he worked every day in the year, of his earning $360.
Why not? This is an international border point where railroads are crossing that run on Sundays as well as other days and an officer has to be there.

Wiil the minister say that he believes that any man can work such hours as to give him $360 overtime out of a possible $399 ?
men not being able to work 12 hours or 14 hours a day, it is to be remembered that they are not engaged in manual labour. A man who is waiting for a train may be lying down on the bench, he may be dozing.

speechtext: At an early hour in the evening when the Minister of Customs was going into his estimates I said that I doubted if he would be able to get many through, but he thought he could convince the opposition of the error of their ways. I think he has had a fair opportunity to do so, and I would suggest that he consider whether
Yes, lots of them.
I am not asking the hon. gentleman.
I do not know any rule of the House which prevents me giving the hon. gentleman much needed information.

The supporters of the government ought to have that confidence in the ministers of the Crown that they will asume they are capable of answering for themselves. I want to refer to another item. A landing waiter at Island Pond receives a salary of $450, and he is paid for overtime $269. That overtime seems to be suspiciously large item in proportion to the salary. Mr. Gendron receives a salary of $450, and $250 for overtime. Mr. Cauchon, preventive officer, receives a salary of $750 and $370 for overtime. These items appear to me to be very doubtful. I hope the minister will be able to give us more satisfactory explanations than he has done.

This overtime comes to us certified by our responsible^ officers, who send the vouchers to the Auditor General. They pass the Auditor General and appear in his books. To my mind the fact that they are in the Auditor General's books is proof positive that the services have been rendered. Whether the time may have exceeded two hours in some cases does not concern me much, because I know and am persuaded that the Auditor General and my officer would not pass accounts unless they were right. When you talk about these
t is worth while sitting any longer.

I did want to get this imount. We have been told by an hon. gen-deman opposite (Mr. Taylor) that there is nothing to criticise in them and that if we svould drop the election Bill they would pass them in two minutes. I view the whole process to-night and this afternoon as an organized effort to stop our getting the money. To-dav is the day on which we issue cheques for the outside service so that they mav reach the distant ports in time. Over 2,000 men who have earned their salaries, many of them receiving small wages, scattered all over the Dominion, about 100 in this city, will not be paid and I am anxious to get them their pay. There is nothing to be gained by the opposition in refusing this amount because there are many items not yet passed if they are determined they should not pass them. I do not think they themselves will feel very well satisfied with what they have done. I would not feel satisfied with myself if I had not made every reasonable effort to pay these men. It is now after four o'clock in the morning and I do not believe in these tests of physical strength, but I did want to make an honest effort to get it, in order that the men might know it was not my fault if they are not paid. I think perhaps I have satisfied them and that they would be unreasonable to ask me to do more than I have. I would like, however, to get it at this afternooi * session.

I want my hon. friend to understand that this is not a Personal attack on him or on his department. W e are

not choosing our time, as he understands, and we all regret that it happens in this way.
You need not have attacked me.

I am sorry for my hon. friend and I think I am speaking for the whole opposition in saying that it is very unfortunate this should fall on him, but we are not choosing which one we will attack or delay.

speechtext:
1.	What action, if any, has the government taken to remedy the reported irregularities in the postal service of Montreal, as complained of by thirty members of the hoard of trade of the city of' Montreal?
2.	Is the government aware that many farms and citizens of the city of Montreal are said to be greatly inconvenienced, and business rnat-terially interfered with, owing to careless handling of mails, delay in delivery of letters,

irregular delivery, carelessness in delivering and handling of papers and packages, and general irregularities said to exist in the postal service of that city? If so, what means have been employed to remedy said grievances?
3 What action, if any, has been taken against the postmaster at Heaslip, Ontario, for reported irregularities and carelessness?
4.	Has there been a new assistant appointed in the Shawville, Quebec, post office? If so, what is his name and salary?

1.	The complaints to which reference is made were not received from individual members of the board of trade, Montreal, but Mr. Geo. Hadrill, secretary of the board of trade, submitted in December, 1906, 28 cases of alleged delay in transmission of mail matter. In 19 of these cases the complaints were not substantiated by evidence or the sender was at fault or the delay was due to causes beyond the control of the department. In dealing with the balance the department pursued its well defined policy of following up the searching inquiry made in each case with prompt measures to make the Montreal postal service in every respect satisfactory. The complaints dealt entirely with the routine of work performed by postal employees and the usual steps were promptly taken to effect the desired improvements for which the machinery of the department was ample and sufficient.
2.	No. Not only is the department not aware that such is the state of affairs, but is positively aware that no such condition exists. The department has had most gratifying evidence from the business men of Montreal in regard to the efficiency of the postal service of that city. It goes without saying that clerical errors will occur and mistakes will be made in a service as large as that of Montreal, but the department ventures to say that there is no city post office on the continent that is giving a better and more faithful service than the post office in the city of Montreal.
As a tribute to the present efficiency of the Montreal postal service the following letter addressed bv Mr. Geo. Hadrill, secretary of the board of Trade, Montreal, to the assistant postmaster, Montreal, under date of the 23rd instant, may be quoted :
Montreal Board of Trade, Montreal, May 23, 1908, to L. J. Gaboury, Esq., assistant postmaster, Montreal.
Sir,-In reply to your inquiry as to whether any complaints have recently been made to this office by members of the board regarding the postal service, I beg to say that with the exception of a letter of recent date pointing out the need of an outside letter box in the post office, no complaints regarding the postal service have been addressed to this office since 1906.
I am, sir, your obedient servant,
(Sgd.) GEO. HADRILL, Secretary.
3.	A complaint was made by Mr. J. H. Field that a registered letter addressed to him at Heaslip was unduly detained at that office. On investigation it was found that the letter in question had been accidentally mislaid by the postmaster of Heaslip, having fallen down behind some pigeon holes in the office, and the postmaster was admonished severely as to his carelessness in the matter. It being the only offence the postmaster was not fined. No other complaints concerning this office have reached the department.
4.	The Post Office Department has nothing to do with the appointment of assistants in post offices like Shawville. The department holds the postmaster responsible for the office being properly carried on and all persons employed in the office are employees, not of the Post Office Department, but of the postmaster at Shawville, who is entirely responsible. When trouble arose a short time ago the postmaster at Shawville was written to that he must provide suitable assistance and he replied that he would employ a suitable assistant at once. Since then no complaints have been made by the public and the department is of the opinion that there is no further ground for complaint.

what was the conclusion to which Mr. Williams came ? After having for a year and a half spent his time and money and the energy and influence of his friends, he finds out that a cabinet minister is ahead of him and has forestalled him in the favourable opinion of the Minister of Agriculture in whose department the matter is ; and he comes naturally and properly to the conclusion that there is no use of his going to the further expenditure of preparing his plans and putting them in unless the minister tells him that he has a chance and that his claim will receive fair and just consideration. With this preference and this great influence against him, he did not file his plans, although he had put in his application at a very early period. On the 3rd of June he writes from St. John to the Hon. Sydney Fisher, Ottawa, Ont.: Dear Sir, I received blanks for application for cold storage warehouse. In your letter of April 11 you gave me to understand that nothing could be done unless plans and specifications were submitted, and you also stated that you looked favourably upon giving this grant in St. John to Sir Frederick Borden. I have already spent considerable of my money going to Ottawa and endeavouring to obtain a grant for the cold storage warehouse in St. John, and I do not feel like spending any more money in getting up plans and specifications if the preference is to be given to Sir Frederick Borden. I have written very strongly on this matter. I would again kindly request that you inform me plainly if it would be worth while proceeding to get plans and specifications ready to submit to you. The answer he got to that, which was his final appeal, was from the deputy minister, saying that if he would submit his application it would receive due consideration. Consequently, although his application was in, he did not file his plans and specifications, which would cost quite a large amount of money, and he had already spent, as he thought, sufficient in the matter. . Now, Sir, this correspondence has divulged the name of Sir Frederick Borden and the company with which he was connected as an applicant for the government subsidy. I propose to trace what had been going on. What had been going on ? Sir Frederick Borden was a member of the cabinet; Hon. Sydney Fisher was a member of the cabinet. Hon. Sydney Fisher and Hon. Sir Frederick Borden and other members of the cabinet sat around the council board and hatched a scheme for government subsidies for cold storage. The very moment they were hatching and bringing out that scheme, Sir Frederick Borden, according to his own letters, was busy getting up a million dollar company In which he had an interest for the very purpose of applying for these government subsidies, which he as a member of the government around the council	board was endeavouring to bring in and having intimate and first knowledge that they would be brought in. I think I shall be able to show that in the meantime the minister was working to get In his application. The first intimation we have of this matter comes from the following letter : L. S.
